#170148. Older adults don’t need to lift heavy weights to build strength

Older adults don’t need to lift heavy weights to build strength

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Strength training with lighter weights may help older adults build strength and maintain muscle mass without heavy lifting.
  • Strength training is recommended for older adults to help maintain muscle, balance and independence.
  • It has been revealed that earlier research has reported that pain and high physical demands can lead older adults to drop out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Strength training with lighter weights may help older adults build strength and maintain muscle mass without heavy lifting.

Strength training is recommended for older adults to help maintain muscle, balance and independence. Heavy loads are commonly used in these programs.

It has been revealed that earlier research has reported that pain and high physical demands can lead older adults to drop out. The authors note that those who drop out often have traits associated with frailty.

A pilot trial in Perth, Western Australia, compared heavy training with lighter training in 40 adults over 55. Strength increased in both groups over 12 weeks.

Neither group revealed a measurable change in muscle mass.

According to recent reports, the study was led by Brett Buist of the School of Human Sciences at the University of Western Australia. Training intensity was chosen by the participants rather than assigned at random.

“Both high- and lower-intensity resistance exercise appears equally effective at improving muscle strength while maintaining muscle mass and quality of life in older adults,” Buist said.

Recent findings suggest that frailty has been linked to falls, hospital admissions, disability and death. Low physical activity and the loss of muscle mass and strength are listed among its common contributors.

Industry observers note that the condition is not always permanent. Ohio State University’s guide to frailty states that it can often be slowed or improved with support.

Industry observers note that low strength is reflected in poorer walking and balance. These changes are known to raise the risk of a fall in older adults.

In a recent development, world Health Organization figures cited in the paper put the share of people over 60 at 12% in 2015. That share is projected to reach 22% by 2050.

In a recent development, lifting weights appears on the National Institute on Aging’s list of strength exercises. The Perth study examined how heavy those weights need to be.

Of the 40 recruits, 33 were women. All participants were living independently in the community.

Sources indicate that sessions were held twice a week at the university under the supervision of exercise physiologists or physiotherapists. Every session included a leg press, a deadlift and a bench press.

Drop jumps from a low box were also performed in each session. The box was about 4 inches (10 centimeters) high, and each landing delivered a firm impact through both feet.

A four-week introductory phase at low-to-moderate intensity was completed by all participants. From week five each person could either move to the heavy program or continue at the lighter level.

In both groups the sets were ended while two to five more repetitions could still have been completed.

Industry observers note that the number of sets multiplied by repetitions was matched closely between the two programs. In this way the load on the bar remained the main difference.

According to recent reports, to be classified as a heavy lifter, a participant had to leg press more than 80% of their estimated maximum. That level had to be reached in at least three out of every four sessions.

Twelve participants met this standard and 14 trained at the lighter level.

By the end of the trial both groups were able to press more weight with their chests and legs. Strength was assessed using the one-repetition maximum, which is the heaviest weight a person can lift once.

Increases in chest press, leg press and leg press relative to body weight were found in each group. Substantial loads were still handled by the lighter group.

Leg press loads in that group averaged about 71% of maximum. Deadlift effort was rated at a median of 5 on a 10-point scale.

Earlier reviews of research in older adults have generally favored heavy lifting for building strength. In some of the studies behind them, heavy training was compared with loads as low as 20% of maximum.

Sources indicate that according to Buist’s team, loads that low were probably insufficient to increase strength. Unequal amounts of total work have also complicated earlier comparisons.

Leg press strength relative to body weight was the only outcome that differed significantly between the groups. However, the authors advised caution when interpreting this result.

“Clinicians can target factors that contribute to frailty using resistance exercise with intensity tailored to individual preferences without compromising outcomes,” said Buist.

Recent findings suggest that neither group indicated a measurable gain in muscle. Lean mass measured by whole-body X-ray scans stayed close to baseline in both programs.

This stability was viewed by the researchers as a useful result because lean mass usually declines with age.

According to recent reports, lean tissue already accounted for about 64% of the volunteers’ body weight at the start. This proportion was higher than in a comparison study cited by the authors.

It has been revealed that no protein supplements were provided during the trial. The training volume was modest as well, with 12 working sets in each session. Some studies that did produce muscle growth used as many as 39 sets.

A small reduction in body fat as a share of total weight was observed in the lighter group. Higher general health scores on the SF-36 survey were reported by the heavy group.

According to recent reports, other scores on the questionnaire changed very little in either group. Most volunteers began between the 50th and 75th percentiles for Australians of their age and sex.

Postural sway was measured on a force plate during standing trials of 30 seconds each. After training the recorded sway path was longer under some of the test conditions.

Recent findings suggest that A longer sway path is normally taken as a sign of poorer balance. However, scores on the 14-item Berg Balance Scale did not decline and balance confidence was maintained.

The authors suggest that participants may have been exploring their limits of stability. Resistance training is known to extend those limits.

The participants who completed the trial were not the group of greatest concern. Of the 39 people tested at baseline, 12 withdrew for reasons including joint pain and holidays.

An average baseline weight of about 162 pounds (73.7 kilograms) was recorded for those who withdrew. Participants who stayed averaged 133 pounds (60.4 kilograms) and had greater leg strength relative to body weight.

Heavier and weaker adults are of particular concern in frailty research, and they were overrepresented among the dropouts.

The final analysis included only 26 people, so small differences between the groups may have been missed. Physical activity outside the supervised sessions was not recorded.

Bonnie Furzer, a co-author from the University of Western Australia, presented the findings as guidance for those who prescribe exercise.

“For older adults who are not tolerating high-intensity resistance and impact training, lowering exercise intensity should be considered to assist adherence whilst maintaining benefits,” stated Furzer.

Longer trials and studies in frail adults have been recommended by the authors.

Until that evidence is available, a weight that people continue to lift may matter more than the heaviest one possible.

The full study was published in the journal Translational Exercise Biomedicine.

#170147. Tech Report: Birdsong has more in common with human speech than scientists expected

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1034 w)

Tech Report: Birdsong has more in common with human speech than scientists expected

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A comparison of 367 bird species and 52 human languages reveals unexpected similarities in the rhythms and patterns of vocal communication.
  • According to recent reports, birds and humans share some surprisingly similar patterns when they make sounds.
  • The finding comes from a comparison of the songs of 367 bird species with people speaking and singing in 52 languages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A comparison of 367 bird species and 52 human languages reveals unexpected similarities in the rhythms and patterns of vocal communication.

According to recent reports, birds and humans share some surprisingly similar patterns when they make sounds. Even birds that never learn their songs naturally produce rhythms much like those found in human speech and music.

The finding comes from a comparison of the songs of 367 bird species with people speaking and singing in 52 languages.

Three patterns of human speech and music appeared across the birds, in those that learn their songs and in those that don’t.

The authors interpret that as a sign that the patterns come from the shared mechanics of making sound rather than from learning alone.

According to recent reports, logan James of McGill University and the University of Texas at Austin led the work with Jon Sakata of McGill. Several co-authors work at McGill’s Centre for Research on Brain, Language and Music.

In an interview with Earth.com, James noted that the shared patterns were what excited the team most.

“These results highlight that, despite the tremendous diversity across human languages and hundreds of species of birds, there are still fundamental shared sequencing patterns,” he remarked.

The recordings came from xeno-canto, where birders around the world upload recordings. The team kept only recordings the recordist had rated top quality and labeled as song rather than calls.

No second species could be in the background, no playback could have been used to provoke the bird, and the singer had to have been seen.

Software then split each song into its separate sounds, and experienced annotators checked every sound. That work produced more than 74,500 individual sounds from about 5,900 songs.

The researchers paired each group of vocal learners with closely related birds that do not learn their songs: songbirds with suboscines, and hummingbirds with nightjars.

On the human side, the team used recordings of people speaking and singing in 52 languages, made for an earlier project.

In human speech and song, the pitch rarely leaps far from one syllable to the next. The team measured the pitch at the end of each bird sound and the start of the next.

Across the birds, the jumps were smaller than chance would produce.

Human voices also keep a beat, with sounds spaced evenly in time.

Birdsong revealed the same pattern more often than would be expected by chance.

And people generally stretch the last sound of a phrase, the way a singer holds a final note.

According to recent reports, birds did that too. Their songs also tended to grow louder through the middle of a phrase and fade at the end, as human music does.

Songbirds have been the usual comparison for human speech because they, like us, learn their songs by listening. This study could set them against close relatives that don’t.

Sakata told Earth.com that the team expected birds that learn their songs to show greater similarities to human speech, since people also learn to speak.

“What surprised us was that the songs of birds that do not learn their songs (e.g., suboscines, nightjars) actually had comparable patterns to us relative to the vocal-learning birds,” he said.

Where vocal learning did make a difference, it did not act the same way in songbirds as in hummingbirds. The authors counted that as no consistent effect.

Sources indicate that the matches were not perfect. Unlike human voices, which tended to become quieter throughout a phrase, birdsong tended to grow louder in the middle before fading at the end.

The authors suspect breathing explains part of it.

According to recent reports, A person usually speaks or sings a whole phrase on one breath, and they suggest that is why the volume drops toward the end. Birds take tiny breaths between the sounds in a song.

Lung size may matter too. Across the birds, bigger species stretched their final sounds more, and a human has much bigger lungs than any of them.

But nightjars, among the largest birds in the study, stretched their final sounds even more than people do, so size can’t explain all of it.

The team also ran a broader measurement of how pitch and rhythm change together across a whole phrase, the same one that separates speech from song in human recordings.

Recent findings suggest that by that measure, bird songs as a group were closer to human speech than to human singing. Hummingbirds and suboscines came out nearest to both, closer than the songbirds.

James said no large group of birds was closest to human patterns overall.

A few species were, on that combined measure, among them the scaled antbird, the blackhead antbird and the rufous-tailed hummingbird.

Songbirds and suboscines did keep a steadier beat than hummingbirds and nightjars, so they are the better birds to study for the roots of human rhythm.

In a commentary published alongside the study, Kazuo Okanoya of Teikyo University wrote that the work gives researchers a basis for testing the mechanisms behind the shared patterns.

“Linguistic concepts can guide such tests but should not be used in place of experimental data,” he added.

The study was based entirely on recordings, so the researchers could not confirm whether similarities in how birds and humans produce sound explain the shared patterns.

It also remains unclear whether listeners’ preferences help shape these patterns.

Sakata said very little is known about the shape of the voice box in many of these species, and that mapping that variety is a next step.

James said earlier work by the group found that people tend to like the same male courtship sounds that females of that species like.

“So we are also curious to examine how much birds (and humans) like the sound of patterns that conform to these universal patterns,” James said.

In a recent development, other features of human music, such as distinct notes and nested layers of structure, have not been checked in birds yet. The authors wrote that those are the next measurements to take.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.
  • Now, scientists have a latest clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a latest clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

In a recent development, such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

Industry observers note that as for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern states. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

According to recent reports, instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” states William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”.

In a recent development, A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these newly introduced ideas, Stern indicates. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 25: Uranus at opposition.

Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

By about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:58 A.M.Sunset: 4:37 P.M.Moonrise: 6:35 P.M.Moonset: 9:33 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

#170144. Industry News: Premature birth may change the brain’s biological clock

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1113 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Premature birth may change the brain’s biological clock

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain scans and donated tissue show that premature birth sets the cerebellum on its own track, leaving it out of step at the due date.
  • Premature birth interrupts a critical period of brain development.
  • Now, researchers have found that even by their original due dates, babies born prematurely show signs of altered development in a key region of the brain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain scans and donated tissue show that premature birth sets the cerebellum on its own track, leaving it out of step at the due date.

Premature birth interrupts a critical period of brain development.

Now, researchers have found that even by their original due dates, babies born prematurely show signs of altered development in a key region of the brain.

The cerebellum of a baby born early matures on a different track. At the due date, its cells are in a different state from a full-term baby’s, according to a new study of brain scans, developmental checkups and donated tissue.

Georgios Sanidas and Gabriele Simonti of Children’s National Hospital in Washington, D.C., led the work.

The study’s senior authors were Panagiotis Kratimenos of Children’s National and the George Washington University School of Medicine and Vittorio Gallo of Seattle Children’s Research Institute.

The tissue came from infants who had died and whose families consented to autopsy, and the authors thank those families in the paper.

In an interview with Earth.com, Kratimenos noted that the work offers parents of preterm babies relief as well as hope.

“Our work reveals that premature birth does not break the brain, nor does it simply pause it,” Kratimenos said.

Between 24 and 40 weeks of pregnancy, the cerebellum grows about fivefold in volume, faster than any other part of the brain.

It handles movement and balance, and it is wired into thinking and language as well.

For a baby born at 26 weeks, much of that growth takes place in a neonatal intensive care unit.

Doctors have known that early birth changes how the cerebellum grows and how a child develops.

What they didn’t know was what happens to the cells inside it, because that can only be studied in human tissue.

The team followed 176 infants born early, none of whom had major brain injury, through scans and checkups.

At the due date, each extra week of pregnancy before birth was worth about 230 cubic millimeters of cerebellum, in proportion to the rest of the brain.

Ultrasound revealed the size gap already in place at 28 weeks. The babies born earliest then grew at the same rate as the rest, so they had not closed it by the due date.

Later checkups showed the same pattern. Between nine months and three years of age, the babies born at the lowest gestational ages were more likely to have motor, thinking and language delays.

A smaller cerebellum went with motor and thinking delays in particular. Lung disease and the other complications of intensive care shaped the numbers, but they didn’t explain them.

To see the cells, the team turned to cerebellar tissue from 83 infants who had died, born anywhere from very early to full term. In 11 of them, the researchers mapped which genes were switched on where.

Three patterns of gene activity tracked how early a baby had been born.

The cerebellum’s most numerous neurons, the small granule cells, were still running an immature program in the babies born earliest.

In babies born closer to term, that program had given way to one built for forming and firing connections.

Under a standard microscope, the granule cells in the earliest-born babies look finished, because they have already reached their adult position.

“Even though those granule cells had reached the right neighborhood, they were still carrying the genetic features of immature cells,” Gallo stated.

The large neurons that carry the cerebellum’s output, the Purkinje cells, were different again.

In the earliest-born infants their genes were tuned to building cell material, with signs of stress, rather than to settling into a mature circuit.

“Being born early forces those same cells to prioritize immediate survival over wiring, leaving them in an unfinished state even months later,” Kratimenos told Earth.com.

Industry observers note that under the microscope, in 77 of the brains, the differences were structural too. A temporary outer layer of brain cell precursors that normally disappears after birth lingered longer in preterm infants.

In full-term infants the density of Purkinje cells fell with age, the normal trimming that refines a circuit. In preterm infants it stayed flat.

The layer that holds the Purkinje cells’ branches grew at the same rate in both groups.

The preterm cerebellum continued to grow without showing the same signs of cellular maturation.

It kept its overall architecture while its development went a different way, which is why a scan that measures size alone may miss it.

Recent findings suggest that preterm babies are assessed, monitored and enrolled in trials by postmenstrual age, the weeks since the mother’s last period. The authors argue that this number measures time, not biological maturity.

Two babies at the same postmenstrual age can be at different developmental stages.

Treatments given around a premature birth, such as magnesium sulfate before delivery and caffeine after it, may therefore act on tissue that differs from one baby to the next.

“To time treatments properly, we have to match our therapies to the biological clock of a baby’s brain cells, rather than their age on the calendar,” Gallo said.

Gallo suggests that therapies designed to promote brain wiring may be less effective before the cells reach the appropriate stage of development.

In a commentary on the paper, Molly Kelly-Goss and Elizabeth Crouch wrote that a preterm infant may follow two calendars.

One is the cerebellum’s physical growth, and the other is the maturation of its cells and molecules.

In their words, “neither captures the true complexity of brain health at the time, nor what it means for the child years later.”.

Sources indicate that the study can’t separate the timing of birth from everything that comes with it. Inflammation, low oxygen and the stress of life outside the womb all arrive together.

The tissue and the scans also came from different infants, since the cerebellum can’t be sampled in a living baby’s brain, and each infant had one MRI scan.

Whether the gap persists, shrinks or is made up later in childhood is not known.

The authors wrote that the same slow maturation that leaves the preterm cerebellum vulnerable may also leave its development open to change for longer.

Gallo mentioned the team’s gene signatures for each stage could guide treatment in two steps.

The first would protect a baby from inflammation and stress in intensive care, and the second would bring in therapies that boost brain wiring once the cells are ready.

Testing that will take studies that time treatments to a baby’s biological stage.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#170143. Power shutoffs meant to prevent wildfires may carry unexpected health risks

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1051 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Power shutoffs meant to prevent wildfires may carry unexpected health risks

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Planned power shutoffs in California were linked to more respiratory-related hospital visits, particularly when wildfire smoke was also present.
  • When the wind picks up on a hot, dry day in fire country, the power company may switch off the electricity on purpose.
  • According to recent reports, A planned shutoff has a cost of its own, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Planned power shutoffs in California were linked to more respiratory-related hospital visits, particularly when wildfire smoke was also present.

When the wind picks up on a hot, dry day in fire country, the power company may switch off the electricity on purpose. A line with no current in it can’t start a fire when it drops into dry brush.

According to recent reports, A planned shutoff has a cost of its own, though. In California, on days when a large shutoff reached a neighborhood, people there were more likely to turn up at an emergency room with a breathing problem.

The rise was largest among people with chronic lung disease, and wildfire smoke in the air at the same time made it larger still.

Lauren Blair Wilner, an epidemiologist at the University of Washington, led the analysis with colleagues at Scripps Institution of Oceanography and Columbia University.

Utilities call these planned outages public safety power shutoffs, or PSPS, and no study before this one had measured what they do to hospital traffic.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wilner pointed to the days when the two overlapped.

“Surprisingly, the effects of a PSPS event and wildfire smoke co-occurring were not simply additive – we found evidence that their effects on health were multiplicative,” she noted.

According to recent reports, three major California utilities serve 88% of the state’s electric customers. They have run these power shutoffs since 2012 and report each one to the California Public Utilities Commission.

The research group PSE Healthy Energy compiled those reports.

Wilner’s team matched the reports for 2013 through 2019, by zip code, against every emergency room visit and unplanned hospital admission by adults across 1,504 California zip codes.

Those records came from the California Department of Health Care Access and Information and included more than 6.6 million visits for breathing problems.

Each visit day was compared with the other days of the same weekday that month, so every patient served as their own comparison.

A large shutoff meant more than 593 customers in a zip code without power.

Industry observers note that on those days, the odds of an emergency room visit or admission for a breathing problem were about 6% higher. Smaller power shutoffs made no measurable difference.

Shutoffs and smoke arrive together more often than not. Of the 11,293 zip-code days with a shutoff, 7,656 also had wildfire smoke in the air.

According to recent reports, asked by Earth.com what else the study revealed, Wilner came back to those overlapping days. “Co-occurrence is what we really need to think about here,” she stated.

Because days with both outnumbered days with a shutoff alone, she added, shutoffs should be studied together with the fires they are meant to prevent.

Recent findings suggest that picture a day with a large shutoff and 10 micrograms of smoke particles in each cubic meter of air. The odds of a breathing-related visit that day were 16% higher than on a day with neither.

The shutoff alone added about 6% and that much smoke alone about 1%, so the pair did more than add up.

The pattern was strongest among people with COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term illness that narrows the airways and makes breathing hard work.

Sources indicate that on days with a large shutoff, the odds of a COPD visit were 29% higher. With smoke on top, they were 37% higher.

Many people with COPD rely on an oxygen concentrator, a machine that pulls oxygen out of room air.

It runs on electricity, and its battery typically lasts three to four hours. A typical shutoff in this study lasted 86 hours, more than three days.

Wilner stated planners should take simultaneous outages into account as they prepare for wildfires and expand healthcare capacity.

“It is essential to put measures in place to ensure that people relying on electricity dependent medical equipment have access to power and can readily access healthcare, if needed,” she said.

Visits for heart problems didn’t rise during shutoffs, with or without smoke, and neither did visits for mental health crises.

Earlier studies of blackouts in Upcoming York State and Florida largely agree, suggesting that outages may be more strongly associated with respiratory problems than heart problems.

How long a shutoff lasted also mattered less than how many people it reached.

When the team counted total hours without power over the previous week instead, they found no link between duration alone and hospital visits.

It has been revealed that each additional 1,000 customers without power, on the other hand, was linked to about 2% higher odds of a breathing-related visit. For COPD visits, the figure was 6%.

Utilities report outages by circuit, so the team can’t say who inside a zip code lost power.

The researchers assumed customers were spread evenly along each circuit, which means some people counted as exposed weren’t.

It has been revealed that nor can the records show whether a patient was home during a shutoff. People may travel to a place that still has power, and breathe more smoke on the way.

Only adults 20 and older who reached a hospital are counted, so anyone who got sick at home and stayed there is missing.

The study covered 2013 to 2019, when planned power shutoffs were less common than they are today.

It has been revealed that since 2022, utilities in Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Hawaii have used shutoffs too. California requires utilities to warn customers first and to open centers where people can charge devices.

Wilner’s team didn’t test whether those centers keep anyone out of the emergency room.

Wilner’s team is turning to what happens after a wildfire or other disaster, when outages and evacuations overlap.

“There are not complete datasets on historical evacuations and power outages after disasters, making it impossible to study the ways in which these things play out and affect health after an event,” she told Earth.com.

Those records, she mentioned, would show what affected communities need and how to reach them.

For now, seven years of California records offer valuable insight into the potential health consequences of planned power shutoffs.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

#170141. Some of the most effective treatments for back pain are also the most affordable

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1404 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Some of the most effective treatments for back pain are also the most affordable

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1404 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A review involving nearly 15,000 people suggests that several drug-free treatments for lower back pain can improve health outcomes and reduce overall costs.
  • Treatments such as yoga, acupuncture, and cognitive therapy might seem like added expenses for people with lower back pain.
  • However, a new review suggests that these approaches can improve health outcomes while reducing overall costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review involving nearly 15,000 people suggests that several drug-free treatments for lower back pain can improve health outcomes and reduce overall costs.

Treatments such as yoga, acupuncture, and cognitive therapy might seem like added expenses for people with lower back pain.

However, a new review suggests that these approaches can improve health outcomes while reducing overall costs.

Researchers reached that conclusion after reviewing 20 papers covering 24 studies and 14,884 people.

Eight treatments that use no drugs and no surgery were both more effective and less costly than usual care in at least one way of counting the costs.

The authors wrote that these treatments are still far from routine in most countries.

It has been revealed that manuela Ferreira, a professor at the George Institute for Global Health in Sydney, was the senior author. Her team included researchers at the University of Sydney and the University of Warwick in England.

“Low back pain is the world’s leading cause of disability, but many effective treatments can also save healthcare dollars,” Ferreira stated.

“Our review found that approaches such as exercise, yoga, acupuncture and psychological support can help people recover while providing good value for money.”.

According to recent reports, pain in the lower back is the leading cause of disability worldwide, and treating it costs a lot. In Australia, back problems accounted for about 2.2% of all health spending in the 2020 to 2021 financial year.

It has been revealed that the team searched ten research databases for studies that compared what a treatment cost with what it achieved. They kept only treatments backed by at least one of three major guidelines.

Those come from the World Health Organization, the United Kingdom’s National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, known as NICE, and the North American Spine Society.

Benefit was measured in a unit that combines how long a person lives with how well they live during that time. Health economists call it a quality-adjusted life year.

The team converted every cost to 2024 British pounds and used the same cutoff NICE uses. A treatment counted as worth paying for if each extra year of healthy life cost less than £20,000.

Twenty papers published between 2005 and 2026 met those criteria.

They covered 24 studies, 55 comparisons with usual care, and 14,884 people in nine high-income countries, most often the United Kingdom.

Usual care in these trials meant ordinary first-contact care: a doctor’s advice, a booklet, some medication, and sometimes a referral to a physical therapist.

Six single treatments came out both more effective and less costly than that.

They were yoga, acupuncture, cognitive therapy, support for people managing their own pain, education aimed at reducing fear of the pain, and mindfulness-based stress reduction.

Two combinations did the same: workplace advice paired with a gradual return to activity, and a program of diet and physical activity.

In an interview with Earth.com, Ferreira was asked what someone with back pain should ask a doctor first. She suggested two questions.

“Is there anything more serious causing my back pain? If not, which is the case for most people, can you teach me or refer me to someone who can teach me how to manage my own symptoms?” she said.

In health economics, a treatment that is both more effective and less costly is described as dominant.

In the whole review, only one comparison went the other way, and that was a British massage program.

Massage cost about £324 more per person than usual care in 2024 money, and it gained no extra healthy time at all.

Whether a treatment saves money depends on whose bills get counted.

The review sorted every result three ways: the health system’s costs, an insurer’s or employer’s costs, and society’s costs, which add in lost wages and missed work.

Industry observers note that A British yoga trial shows why that matters. In it, 313 people with chronic or recurring back pain were offered 12 weekly group classes.

Counting only health care, the classes added about £715 per person, and each extra year of healthy life cost about £19,300, just under the £20,000 bar.

Sources indicate that counting lost workdays too, the yoga group cost society about £293 less per person than the usual-care group. And the yoga group still gained more healthy time.

The biggest saving in the review came from a Dutch program for workers on sick leave with chronic back pain.

It paired workplace advice with a gradual return to activity, and it cut society’s costs by about £7,315 per person compared with usual care. An Australian cognitive therapy program cut them by about £2,671.

Savings like those count only when lost work is part of the sum.

A treatment did not have to save money to be considered cost-effective.

Counting the health system’s costs, 14 of 18 comparisons passed, including exercise alone, spinal manipulation, and exercise paired with cognitive therapy.

Counting society’s costs, 15 of 19 passed, and counting an insurer’s or employer’s, 11 of 14 did. Passing was the rule, but confidence in each pass varied.

Where a study reported how likely its treatment was to be good value, the figure ran from 50% to 99.6%.

One of the clearest savings came from an enhanced course of acupuncture in the United States, with extra sessions added to a standard 12-week course. It cut health care costs by about £396 per person.

Acupuncture and massage were tested in many of the studies, and their results were inconsistent.

Sources indicate that the authors wrote that this points to context, who is paying, and how the treatment is delivered. A Belgian modeling study found osteopathy was dominant from a payer’s perspective.

It has been revealed that the three modeling studies in the review met far fewer items on their quality checklist than the trials met on theirs, though. The weakest of them met two of 57 items.

A review in 2011 of 26 studies reached a similar verdict on some of these treatments, including exercise, acupuncture, and cognitive behavioral therapy.

Nine fresh economic evaluations have come out since the most recent review of the topic, in 2019.

The authors wrote that theirs is the first to cover every treatment the current guidelines recommend, measured against usual care.

Ferreira’s team wrote that yoga, acupuncture, cognitive behavioral therapy, and treatments aimed at reducing fear and stress still aren’t routinely offered or paid for in most countries.

Working out why, the team wrote, should be the next focus.

Asked what surprised her most, Ferreira said it was that these treatments are not always available to patients.

“I was pleased to see so many options can benefit both patients and society,” Ferreira noted.

“The good news for people with back pain is that some of the most effective treatments are also among the most cost-effective.”.

“Investing in evidence-based care such as exercise, physical therapies and psychological support could help more people get better while reducing pressure on health systems.”.

Every one of the 24 studies came from a high-income country, so the authors wrote that their findings are unlikely to carry over to lower-income settings.

Ferreira said testing them in poorer countries would take upcoming trials and studies with local patients, clinicians, and policymakers.

Those would check that the treatments are safe, suited to local conditions, and acceptable.

Costs are tied to the health system that recorded them, and the studies measured them too differently to pool into one estimate.

Some people were left out by design. Studies of sciatica, where the pain runs down the leg, weren’t included, and neither were people who had back surgery in the past year.

Out-of-pocket costs, community services, and lost work were reported less often than the treatment’s price.

The larger gap is in what the review had nothing to compare. Not one of the studies that met its criteria tested a drug, an injection, or an operation for chronic pain in the back. Those treatments are paid for all over the world.

“We have not found studies on guideline endorsed pharmacological or surgical interventions for low back pain and therefore highlight the urgent need for those as well,” Ferreira told Earth.com.

The authors wrote that future studies should count lost work and community costs too.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

#170140. Industry News: Nov. 26, 2018: Mars InSight lander touches down

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (381 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Astronomy ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Nov. 26, 2018: Mars InSight lander touches down

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (381 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that inSight, short for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport, landed on Mars Nov.
  • Sources indicate that in addition to bountiful seismic data, which included more than 1,300 marsquakes, InSight recorded about a year’s worth of weather data at the lander’s location with unprecedented accuracy, according to Bruce Banerdt, the mission’s principal investigator and principal research scientist.
  • According to recent reports, not everything was a rousing success, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that inSight, short for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport, landed on Mars Nov. 26, 2018, tasked with a simple yet challenging mission: unlock the mysteries of Mars’ interior. Top priorities included uncovering Mars’ internal structure by measuring the thickness of the crust, obtaining the size and density of the core, and sussing out the structure and composition of Mars’ mantle.

Sources indicate that in addition to bountiful seismic data, which included more than 1,300 marsquakes, InSight recorded about a year’s worth of weather data at the lander’s location with unprecedented accuracy, according to Bruce Banerdt, the mission’s principal investigator and principal research scientist. The InSight lander also took the first magnetic field measurements on the surface of Mars and measured several properties of the soil around it.

According to recent reports, not everything was a rousing success, however. Most famously, the mission’s “mole” subsurface probe only penetrated about 16 inches (40 centimeters) deep, despite being designed to burrow to a depth of at least 3 feet (10 meters). It turned out that the soil beneath InSight’s struts was unlike any previously encountered on the surface; it simply didn’t cooperate with the instrument’s design. But even that cloud has a silver lining, as it provided scientists with notable details about the terrain upon which InSight landed.

InSight’s successful initial two-year mission was extended to run at least through the end of December 2022. But the stationary lander relied on power generated from its two large solar panels, which steadily gathered dust. That dust reduced the panels’ efficiency over time, forcing mission planners to make tough choices regarding power allotment. In May of 2022, engineers placed the craft’s robotic arm into a final resting pose and turned off all its instruments, save one: InSight’s seismometer continued to operate on what little power was available, running about half the time, according to Banerdt. InSight last contacted Earth Dec. 15, 2022, after which two attempts were made to raise the lander. Both failed, and a few days later, NASA officially brought the mission to a close.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A striking Landsat 9 image reveals the snow-covered summit and active lava dome of Shivelyuch volcano on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula.
  • Today’s Image of the Day features one of Russia’s most active volcanoes rising above a blanket of clouds on the Kamchatka Peninsula.
  • Snow covers the upper slopes of Shivelyuch, while a dark formation near the summit offers a glimpse of the volcanic activity taking place within the mountain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A striking Landsat 9 image reveals the snow-covered summit and active lava dome of Shivelyuch volcano on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula.

Today’s Image of the Day features one of Russia’s most active volcanoes rising above a blanket of clouds on the Kamchatka Peninsula.

Snow covers the upper slopes of Shivelyuch, while a dark formation near the summit offers a glimpse of the volcanic activity taking place within the mountain.

The image was captured on November 8, 2026, by the Operational Land Imager aboard Landsat 9. Although clouds concealed much of the surrounding landscape, the volcano’s summit remained visible from space.

The contrast between the snowy mountainside and the exposed volcanic rock offers a striking portrait of a landscape that is continually being rebuilt from within.

Shivelyuch, also known as Shiveluch, is among the largest and most active volcanoes on the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia’s Far East.

According to recent reports, the mountain has a complex geological history. Its older structure, known as Stary Shiveluch, dates back roughly 65,000 years.

A younger volcanic complex, Molodoy Shiveluch, subsequently developed within the remains of the older mountain.

The Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program has documented at least 60 major eruptions at Shivelyuch during the Holocene, the geological epoch that began approximately 11,700 years ago.

It has been revealed that successive eruptions and collapses have left extensive deposits of volcanic material across the surrounding terrain. These deposits preserve a record of the mountain’s turbulent past.

One of the most intriguing features of Shivelyuch is its enormous caldera, a depression measuring approximately 5.6 miles (nine kilometers) across.

Within this depression, a lava dome has developed as magma reaches the surface. The dome stands out against the snow in the satellite image.

Unlike the fluid lava commonly associated with Hawaiian volcanoes, the thick lava that builds volcanic domes does not travel easily across the landscape.

Instead, it accumulates around the opening from which it emerges.

As more material reaches the surface, the dome can expand, develop fractures, and become increasingly unstable.

It has been revealed that sections of these domes sometimes collapse. Such events can unleash pyroclastic flows – rapidly moving mixtures of scorching gas, ash, and fragmented rock that sweep down a volcano’s slopes.

The process can dramatically alter the appearance of a mountain, sometimes within minutes.

Kamchatka’s extraordinary volcanic landscape owes its existence to the movement of enormous sections of Earth’s outer shell.

The peninsula sits along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a vast region of geological activity surrounding much of the Pacific Ocean.

Here, the Pacific tectonic plate descends beneath another plate in a process called subduction.

Water released from the descending plate promotes melting in the overlying mantle, generating magma that can eventually rise toward the surface.

Over millions of years, this process has created a remarkable concentration of volcanoes, along with hot springs, geysers, and other geothermal features.

Kamchatka provides scientists with an opportunity to observe some of the fundamental processes responsible for reshaping Earth’s surface.

The effects of volcanic activity at Shivelyuch can extend well beyond the peninsula.

Although volcanic ash resembles ordinary dust, it consists of tiny fragments of rock, minerals, and volcanic glass.

These abrasive particles can damage aircraft engines and other critical equipment.

High-altitude winds can carry ash clouds across international borders and oceans. In July 2026, ash from Shivelyuch reached Alaskan airspace after traveling across the Bering Sea, disrupting air travel.

Even between major explosions, previously deposited ash can become airborne again when strong winds sweep across the landscape.

This means that an ash plume does not necessarily indicate that a new explosive eruption has occurred.

Volcanic activity at Shivelyuch had persisted for several months when Landsat 9 acquired this image.

Monitoring a remote volcano surrounded by unpredictable weather presents considerable challenges.

Satellites offer scientists an invaluable perspective on places where direct observations are difficult.

In addition to capturing changes in the appearance of volcanic landscapes, instruments aboard some satellites can detect infrared radiation associated with unusually hot surfaces.

These measurements help researchers identify areas of elevated temperature that may be associated with freshly exposed lava or other volcanic activity.

By comparing observations collected over extended periods, scientists can also track the growth and destruction of lava domes, map volcanic deposits, and document changes to the surrounding environment.

Weather clouds can interfere with many of these observations, making clear views of active volcanic features particularly valuable.

Sources indicate that seen from hundreds of miles above Earth, Shivelyuch appears almost serene. Its snow-covered slopes emerge from the clouds, revealing a rugged summit seemingly isolated from the world below.

Yet the mountain’s appearance belies the geological activity taking place beneath its surface.

The dark lava dome visible in today’s image represents the latest chapter in a history of destruction and renewal spanning thousands of years.

Long after the surrounding clouds have dispersed, the forces responsible for building Shivelyuch will continue to transform the mountain.

Narwhals may have a hidden vulnerability as the Arctic warms

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Narwhals and seals rely on the same Arctic fish, but warming waters could leave narwhals with fewer options.
  • According to recent reports, A narwhal and a seal do not appear to have much in common.
  • In one Arctic fjord, however, the summer diets of these animals share a great deal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Narwhals and seals rely on the same Arctic fish, but warming waters could leave narwhals with fewer options.

According to recent reports, A narwhal and a seal do not appear to have much in common. The narwhal is a whale with a long spiral tusk. It can also dive much deeper than most seals.

In one Arctic fjord, however, the summer diets of these animals share a great deal.

Four marine mammals share those waters each summer. A fresh study found that narwhals, ringed seals and harp seals all lean heavily on one small fish, polar cod.

Sources indicate that of the group, narwhals had the narrowest diet. That could leave them with the least room to adjust if warming changes the fjord’s prey.

Monica Ogawa led the research. She’s a specially appointed assistant professor at Japan’s National Institute of Polar Research. She is also affiliated with the Arctic Research Center at Hokkaido University.

“Our findings provide further insights into potential changes in the Arctic marine ecosystem associated with climate change,” Ogawa said.

Recent findings suggest that the fjord is called Inglefield Bredning, or Kangerlussuaq in Greenlandic. It lies in northwest Greenland. About 700 Inuit live in three settlements along its shores: Qaanaaq, Qeqertat and Siorapaluk.

Recent findings suggest that hunting marine mammals is how people there make a living. These animals are hard to watch while they feed underwater. So the team checked what they had already eaten.

Stomachs were collected over three summers, from 2022 to 2024. They came from animals taken in regular subsistence hunts, within existing rules and quotas. Local hunters and biologists did the collecting.

Sources indicate that in all, 126 stomachs were gathered. Ringed seals supplied 54, harp seals 17, bearded seals 23 and narwhals 32. Each stomach’s contents were washed through a series of sieves, and every item was identified.

Sources indicate that how big were the fish? To find out, the team measured tiny ear stones found inside fish heads.

“The collection of a large number of stomach samples would not have been possible without the cooperation of local Inuit hunters,” Ogawa said.

“Continued sample collection through collaboration with hunters will play an notable role in the long-term monitoring of Arctic marine ecosystems.”.

Sources indicate that in total, 62 types of prey were identified in the stomachs. These included 27 species of fish and 19 species of shrimp. Clams and snails were also recorded, along with squid and tiny drifting animals.

In a recent development, polar cod was found more often than any other prey. It was the main food of ringed seals, harp seals and narwhals.

Industry observers note that polar cod was present in 77.5% of ringed seal stomachs that contained food. By estimated weight it made up 82.1% of their diet.

The narwhal results were similar. Polar cod and one closely related fish accounted for 93% of the prey weight in narwhals. Squid or related animals were present in 88.9% of narwhal stomachs with food.

According to recent reports, the diets were then compared between species. A meaningful overlap was found between ringed seals and harp seals. Harp seals and narwhals overlapped to a similar degree.

“The dietary niches of all species, excluding bearded seals, substantially overlapped, suggesting a high potential for interspecific competition,” Ogawa said.

The polar cod eaten by narwhals averaged about 4.7 inches (119 mm). Seals ate larger polar cod that averaged 6.4 to 7 inches (163 to 179 mm).

Narwhals also ate much more of a second fish. It is known as Arctic cod and is sometimes called ice cod. This fish is most often found between about 660 and 2,600 feet (200 and 800 meters) deep.

Narwhals can dive deeper than 2,600 feet. In this fjord they have repeatedly collided with research equipment moored at about 1,300 feet (400 meters).

In a recent development, this behavior suggests that narwhals may feed close to the seafloor. The authors propose that narwhals may use their diving ability to reach fish in deep water. In this way they could avoid competing with seals for the larger polar cod.

The diets of individual narwhals were also much more alike than those of individual seals. Narwhals were the only species in which this similarity was large enough to be considered ecologically meaningful.

Recent findings suggest that narwhals had already been ranked by earlier studies among the Arctic mammals most at risk from warming. Their limited range of prey is one reason for this.

Industry observers note that greater variation was found among seals, even within a single species. Seal pups ate smaller cod than older seals. Young ringed seals ate more tiny drifting animals and moved toward polar cod as they grew older.

The widest diet was recorded in bearded seals. A total of 52 types of prey were found in their stomachs. No meaningful overlap was found between their diet and those of the other three species.

In a recent development, sculpins were the main prey of bearded seals. These are spiny fish that live on the seabed. Clams and snails were present in 70.6% of bearded seal stomachs with food. They were not found in any of the other species.

Recent findings suggest that most of the bearded seals were taken in shallow water where the seafloor can be reached easily. The shrimp they ate also lived on the bottom. In contrast, narwhals ate shrimp that live in open water in deeper areas.

Bearded seals are considered by the authors to be the most resilient of the four species. “Overall, dietary specialization and age structure emerge as key determinants of ecological resilience in marine mammals,” Ogawa mentioned.

Sources indicate that something else turned up in the stomachs. It hints that the fjord itself may be changing.

Earlier studies were done here from 1938 to 1941 and again in 1998. Back then, the tiny drifting animal seals ate most was a cold-water crustacean called an amphipod.

The cold-water amphipod species recorded in earlier studies tends to avoid water warmer than about 36°F (2°C).

This time, krill were the most common drifting animal in ringed seal stomachs. Krill had never been recorded before in marine mammal stomachs from Inglefield Bredning.

It has been revealed that the krill species found here can handle warmer conditions. They’re spreading north as Arctic seas heat up.

According to recent reports, redfish turned up too, in bearded seals. This fish comes from more southern waters and is moving north. It hadn’t been recorded as prey in this area before.

Industry observers note that no such change was seen in narwhals or harp seals, compared with older studies. That difference may reflect how flexible each species’ diet is, the authors suggest.

A stomach highlights only an animal’s last few meals. It can’t tell us how a narwhal eats across a whole year.

Industry observers note that the fjord’s cast also changes with the seasons. Narwhals and harp seals leave in winter. Once sea ice returns, walruses arrive. So the study is really a summer snapshot from one fjord.

According to recent reports, harp seals may become important in this story. At present they visit the fjord only during summer. Warming is expected to push them farther north and keep them there for longer periods.

According to the authors, competition for the same cod could then develop among the three species.

How many cod live in the fjord, and where do they gather? The team doesn’t know yet. That information could help determine whether seals and narwhals actually compete for food.

It has been revealed that stomachs can’t show how deep each animal hunted, either. The authors called for tags that record each animal’s dives. A survey of the fish themselves is needed too.

“Building on the findings of this study, we hope to better understand how Arctic marine ecosystems will change in the future and how these changes may affect marine mammals and the local communities that depend on them,” Ogawa said.

It has been revealed that future studies could test whether narwhals would switch prey if polar cod and Arctic cod decline. That decline is expected as Atlantic fish move north.

The full study was published in the journal Marine Ecology Progress Series.

Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Industry observers note that kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Major Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

In a recent development, we first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the issue near and dear to his heart: health care.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss indicates. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

According to recent reports, several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

According to recent reports, romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance strategy in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

According to recent reports, the podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

According to recent reports, overall, Mitt & Ted gave me latest appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

Recent findings suggest that “The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss states. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”.

#170134. Surrounded by female cows, a bull named Achille chose to form a close bond with a male donkey named Patroclo that lasted for weeks, leaving scientists baffled

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1186 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Surrounded by female cows, a bull named Achille chose to form a close bond with a male donkey named Patroclo that lasted for weeks, leaving scientists baffled

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Achille the bull and Patroclo, a male donkey, mated and groomed each other for weeks in an Ethiopian pasture, forming a very unusual and mutual bond.
  • On a beautiful plateau in Ethiopia, a bull named Achille spent his days in a pasture full of female cows and other bulls.
  • This happened not once, not twice, but at least 51 times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Achille the bull and Patroclo, a male donkey, mated and groomed each other for weeks in an Ethiopian pasture, forming a very unusual and mutual bond.

On a beautiful plateau in Ethiopia, a bull named Achille spent his days in a pasture full of female cows and other bulls. Yet over two weeks in March, researchers watched him ignore the females, and his own species, to mount a male donkey named Patroclo.

This happened not once, not twice, but at least 51 times.

Male cattle sometimes mount each other when no female cows are around, but Achille had plenty of them right beside him, and Patroclo never tried to get away.

The researchers concluded that the pair shared a selective, mutual bond, and that the mounting was part of it.

Elisabetta Palagi, an associate professor of biology at the University of Pisa in Italy, and her colleagues described the pair in a two-page report.

Martina Francesconi and André da Cruz, both PhD students at Pisa, are the lead authors. Da Cruz is also affiliated with CRIA, an anthropology research center in Lisbon.

Their report focuses on this one bull and one donkey, who they watched and studied very closely for eight days.

According to recent reports, in an interview with Earth.com, Palagi remarked the team discovered the pair unexpectedly. They were in Ethiopia studying geladas, a kind of monkey, for a University of Pisa project called BRIDGES.

“It is a lovely reminder that careful field observation can reveal questions we had never thought to ask,” she mentioned.

According to recent reports, the pasture is in Debre Libanos, in Ethiopia’s Oromia region. Achille and Patroclo belonged to different owners. They met only during the day, when cattle and donkeys shared the pasture in mixed herds.

In a recent development, at night, Achille was housed with another adult bull, a cow, and a calf. Patroclo was housed with two other male donkeys.

In a recent development, both animals had other possible partners in the same pasture. On any given day, there were three to six bulls and three to seven cows. There were also three male donkeys and two to seven female donkeys.

When the bull and the donkey kept interacting, Palagi stated, the team began documenting the pair systematically.

The researchers recorded how Achille and Patroclo behaved toward each other and toward the rest of the herd. They kept recording even when nothing sexual was happening.

In all, the team saw the two together on four days and apart on four more.

In a recent development, thirty-four of the 51 mounts included penetration. The researchers saw no avoidance and no aggression between the two animals.

Asked what surprised her most, Palagi named two things. One was how selective the two animals were about each other. The other was how actively Patroclo took part.

“What initially looked like an unusual encounter turned out to be a persistent pattern of preferential interaction,” Palagi told Earth.com.

Industry observers note that patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and nipped him. Twice, another bull tried to come near Patroclo. Patroclo chased and bit him.

Industry observers note that the two animals also licked, rubbed, and nuzzled each other. The team looked closely at the six seconds or so around each mount.

In a recent development, in about a quarter of the mounts, that friendly contact happened just before. In nearly three-quarters, it happened just after.

Contact before a mount isn’t a surprise, the authors wrote, because it may make mounting easier. Contact afterward is harder to explain. It appears to keep the social interaction going after sex is over.

Palagi noted Achille and Patroclo had friendly contact with each other more often than with other animals, and it lasted longer.

Recent findings suggest that the two also stayed close. When both were in the pasture, they spent more time near each other than apart.

According to recent reports, achille approached and mounted another male donkey only twice. That donkey avoided him and flattened its ears, a threatening expression.

When Achille tried to mount the other donkey, Patroclo moved toward Achille. Achille immediately stopped and directed his friendly behavior at Patroclo instead.

Sources indicate that the researchers also analyzed Patroclo’s facial expressions using a coding system developed for horses. They compared four situations: Achille mounting him, Achille making friendly contact, Achille standing close by, and Patroclo alone.

Industry observers note that across all four, Patroclo’s face showed no detectable difference. To the team, that suggests Patroclo didn’t see Achille as a threat.

In a recent development, achille courted cows the way bulls usually do, but he never tried to mount one. The other bulls nearby may have discouraged him, the researchers wrote.

After similar courtship with Patroclo, Achille did mount him.

Sources indicate that the one time another bull tried to mount Achille, Achille rejected him. Among the rest of the herd, the team recorded no mounting between cattle and donkeys during the study.

Same-sex sexual behavior is widespread in animals. It has been documented in several species of the horse family.

Industry observers note that but the team couldn’t find a published report of such behavior in donkeys. They also found no report of a lasting sexual relationship between domestic hoofed animals of two different species.

Classic explanations for same-sex sexual behavior include one animal forcing another, mistaken identity, and a shortage of opposite-sex partners.

The authors wrote that none of these seems to fully explain Achille and Patroclo. Their relationship was selective and mutual.

Recent findings suggest that A bond like this must also come at a cost. The two spent time and energy on each other that could have gone into producing offspring. To the authors, the strength of the bond seems to outweigh that cost.

“Their relationship reminds us that sexual behavior can be part of a social bond beyond reproduction, and that these bonds can cross species boundaries,” Palagi noted.

Nobody knows yet what the bond does for either animal. The behavior may benefit one or both of them directly. Or it may be a result of the way cattle and donkeys form social bonds.

Palagi mentioned the team can’t tell whether sex helped keep the bond going or came out of an attachment the two animals already had.

Industry observers note that domestication may have played a part in the behavior too. The authors wrote that it changes animals’ social settings and their chances to interact with other species.

The next step, Palagi remarked, is to find out how often relationships like this one occur and to follow them over time.

In a recent development, she suggested comparing friendly behavior and signs of tension before and after sex. That could help test whether sex is linked to keeping a relationship going or to easing tension.

The team would also need to observe different pairs in different social settings to tell those two possibilities apart, she said.

The full study was published in the journal Current Biology.
