President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO mentioned Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

It has been revealed that white House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting newly introduced ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray stated in a statement.

It has been revealed that sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”.

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters mentioned.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

It has been revealed that "To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad.".

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he noted the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

According to recent reports, and Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman remarked in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

Industry observers note that he served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

According to recent reports, before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

According to recent reports, former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

In a recent development, david M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Industry observers note that gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide at the moment serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. #170132. The closest exoplanets may host magnetic fields

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1409 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Astronomy ↗ Open Full Page

The closest exoplanets may host magnetic fields

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in all the universe, Earth is the only planet known to have life.
  • But Earth is far from the only planet we know of.
  • Sources indicate that because of their protective role, magnetic fields have major implications in the search for life beyond Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in all the universe, Earth is the only planet known to have life. A major part of the reason life is possible here is our planet’s magnetic field. It acts like a shield, deflecting harmful energy from our Sun as well as cosmic rays from deep space that could otherwise erode Earth’s atmosphere and irradiate the surface, a death sentence for evolving life-forms.

But Earth is far from the only planet we know of. As of this writing, there are more than 6,300 confirmed exoplanets on the roster, with more added by the day. Scientists have discovered stars with as many planets as our own Sun hosts. In other systems, planets as major as Jupiter whip around their sun in only a few days’ time. Astronomers have even discovered planets that orbit multiple stars at once, and they recently caught a glimpse of a possible atmosphere around a rocky, Earth-sized world in its star’s habitable zone. But until 2026, they had no compelling evidence that any terrestrial exoplanets had magnetic fields of their own.

Sources indicate that because of their protective role, magnetic fields have major implications in the search for life beyond Earth. Astronomers have long suspected that part of the reason Mars now appears dead is that its magnetic field fizzled out billions of years ago. This let the solar wind strip the water and other volatile compounds from its atmosphere, leaving it cold and barren.

Beyond the solar system, in 2019 researchers reported “indirect detections of exoplanetary magnetic fields” in four hot Jupiters. Then, a 2021 study found a strong signature of a magnetic field around HAT-P-11 b, a Neptune-like planet. Two years later, a pair of studies detected possible signs of a magnetic field around YZ Ceti b — this time, a rocky, Earth-like planet roughly the same size as, and only a bit less massive than our own. But this find has not yet been confirmed.

In a recent development, in July 2026, a study published in Astronomy & Astrophysics found possible evidence of magnetic fields around two rocky exoplanets. Not just any exoplanets, either — Proxima Centauri b and d, the closest confirmed planets beyond our solar system, orbiting the red dwarf Proxima Centauri 4.2 light-years away.

Proxima b, roughly Earth’s mass and size, orbits every 11.1 days. Proxima d, likely a quarter to a third of our planet’s mass and 70% its size, orbits closer in with a period of 5.1 days. Because Proxima Centauri is smaller and less massive than our Sun, Proxima b is inside the habitable zone, where temperatures allow liquid surface water. A third planet, Proxima c, was tentatively detected in 2019 but is still unconfirmed. Astronomers don’t yet know if any of these worlds host atmospheres.

In a recent development, the fresh study, led by María Rosa Zapatero Osorio of the Centro de Astrobiología in Madrid, Spain, used 117 separate observations made with the Echelle SPectrograph for Rocky Exoplanets and Stable Spectroscopic Observations (ESPRESSO) instrument on the Very Large Telescope atop Cerro Paranal in Chile. The research followed up on previous studies conducted with ESPRESSO in 2020 and 2022, which focused on confirming the presence of planets around Proxima Centauri. Zapatero Osorio and her collaborators used the data to identify a peculiar correlation between the timing of flares emitted from Proxima Centauri and the orbital periods of its planets.

“We detected low-energy flares occurring with a characteristic period of about 5.1 days,” Zapatero Osorio says. “This is very close to Proxima d’s orbital period.” But flares did not occur during every orbit of Proxima d, so the team ran statistical analyses to determine whether the flares were preferentially occurring at particular phases of the planet’s orbit. They found strong statistical evidence “that the occurrence of the flares is not randomly distributed over the planet’s orbital period,” Zapatero Osorio says. “Instead, a significant number of flares tend to occur at particular times in Proxima d’s orbit.” This is a possible indication that Proxima d could be interacting magnetically with its parent star, which would be likely to happen if the planet has a strong magnetic field of its own.

Using a model adapted from the physics of solar flares, Zapatero Osorio’s team calculated that Proxima d could have a magnetic field anywhere from 8 to 230 gauss in strength, with the best median estimate limited to around 16 gauss. This is about 27 times more powerful than Earth’s magnetic field (0.6 gauss), which protects life on Earth from the worst of the Sun’s energy.

Industry observers note that their model assumes that the star and planet are magnetically connected, Zapatero Osorio notes. Each sustains its own magnetic field, and these fields are interconnected. As a result of this connection, stress builds up on the stellar surface. From time to time, this stress is released in the form of low-energy flares, whose period is closely tied to the planet’s orbital period.

Sources indicate that although there was not as strong a correlation between Proxima b’s orbital period and the stellar flares, the team did find that Proxima b could also be interacting with the star, albeit in a lesser capacity. This suggests that although the finding is less sure, Proxima b may also sustain a magnetic field.

Recent findings suggest that there are alternative explanations for the findings. One possibility is that there could be intrinsic, long-lived active regions on Proxima Centauri itself that account for the peculiar timing of the flares. Another explanation is that gravitational interactions between the planets and Proxima Centauri could induce disturbances on the star without requiring a strong planetary magnetosphere, although the team suggests this is less likely. It’s also possible that when Proxima’s stellar wind reaches the planets, it interacts with them in a way that mimics the effects of a planetary magnetic field without requiring one.

Like most red dwarfs, Proxima is a highly active star, regularly belching out intense flares that would be hazardous to any fledgling life-forms on the worlds in close orbit. Because Proxima is so close to Earth and has at least one rocky planet in its habitable zone, it makes a perfect testbed for studying how stellar flares could affect habitability around red dwarfs — the most common stars in the universe.

Astronomers looking for habitable worlds around these stars must contend with the likelihood that any planets would be effectively sterilized by the intense radiation in the flares constantly washing over them. Now, though, there is a glimmer of hope. If Proxima b and d do have magnetic fields, as this research suggests, they could act much like Earth’s own protective magnetic shield, deflecting enough harmful stellar radiation that life might just be able to take hold.

Industry observers note that “Earth’s magnetic field plays an important role in protecting life and supporting human progress,” says Zapatero Osorio. “It shields our planet from the solar wind and energetic particles, and it has also played an important role in navigation.”.

In a recent development, unfortunately, Proxima d is so close to its host star that it is likely too hot to sustain life as we know it. Proxima b, however, lies within the habitable zone. “Based on the results of our study, both Proxima d and b may have magnetospheres capable of providing some protection against their host star’s activity,” Zapatero Osorio indicates.

Recent findings suggest that the importance of this find goes deeper than simply a pair of neighboring planets. In the last few years, evidence has emerged that gas giant exoplanets similar to Jupiter and Saturn host magnetic fields. These are the easiest types of planets to detect and study, but while magnetic fields around such worlds are certainly fascinating, the implications for planetary habitability are limited.

Sources indicate that but as the number of known planets continues to swell, so, too, does our sample of Earth-like worlds. And if the two closest rocky planets beyond our solar system do indeed have magnetic fields, then perhaps these features are common. If true, it increases the chances that rocky worlds across the galaxy could be habitable — at least, for life-forms as we understand them. And the more planets capable of hosting life, the more likely it is that we might someday discover we are not alone.

Nick Oakes is a science writer for NASA’s Heliophysics Education Activation Team at Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.

#170131. Tech Report: Smartwatch screens are too small to pinch and zoom, so engineers turned the forearm into a touchpad

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1099 w)

Tech Report: Smartwatch screens are too small to pinch and zoom, so engineers turned the forearm into a touchpad

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A radar wristband turns the forearm into a smartwatch touchpad that reads two-finger gestures and press force, beating a touchscreen in tests.
  • On a phone, pinching to zoom or scrolling with two fingers is second nature.
  • Engineers have now moved those gestures off the screen and onto the skin of the forearm, turning it into a touchpad for the smartwatch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A radar wristband turns the forearm into a smartwatch touchpad that reads two-finger gestures and press force, beating a touchscreen in tests.

On a phone, pinching to zoom or scrolling with two fingers is second nature. On a watch face the size of a postage stamp, there is no room for it.

Engineers have now moved those gestures off the screen and onto the skin of the forearm, turning it into a touchpad for the smartwatch.

Recent findings suggest that A small radar on a wristband points at the skin next to the watch. Fingers pressing there leave tiny dents, and the radar reads where the fingers are, how many there are, and whether a press is gentle or firm.

In tests with 20 volunteers, the system recognized gestures about 93 percent of the time after a calibration of under four minutes. In a head-to-head task, people missed their targets less often on their own arm than on a watch touchscreen.

The work comes from Chenhan Xu, an assistant professor of computer science at North Carolina State University, and doctoral student Yuliang Fu, with Rakshita Ranganath and Huining Li. They call the system EpiPad.

“Smartwatch screens are too small for the touch interactions people use every day on phones and laptops, such as two-finger scrolling, pinch-to-zoom, or pressing harder to trigger a different command,” Xu said.

“Our goal was to develop a small, wearable technology that would provide that level of interactive control for people.”.

On a watch touchscreen, a fingertip covers a small target it is trying to tap. The authors wrote that a typical on-screen keyboard on a commercial smartwatch gives each key about 0.12 inches (3 millimeters) of width.

Earlier attempts to use the forearm skin as a touchpad mostly tracked a single finger, or relied on landmarks such as knuckles, which limited taps to a few fixed spots.

Rotating, zooming, and other two-finger moves were out of reach.

The back of the forearm offered room to work with. The system turns a strip of forearm skin about 6 inches by 1.6 inches (15 by 4 centimeters) into a touchpad input area. The padding of muscle under that skin makes a hard press comfortable.

The sensor is a millimeter-wave radar chip with one transmitting antenna and three receiving ones. It sends out a pulse every thousandth of a second and times the reflections.

Because the radar faces across the skin from the side, a press straight down barely changes the distance it measures.

So the team mounted the chip about 0.55 inches (14 millimeters) above the skin, roughly the thickness of a chunky smartwatch case, and angled it slightly downward.

“With the EpiPad, a compact millimeter-wave radar worn on a wristband reads the tiny dents fingertips make as they press the skin, so the system tracks multiple fingers and how hard each one presses,” stated Fu, the paper’s first author.

The system distinguishes two levels of pressure, gentle and hard. The hard press is where the signal gets tricky, because a finger arriving on the skin shifts the radar reading in the same way the dent does.

The team found the pressure signature in the moment the finger holds still after landing.

The 20 volunteers, 14 men and six women, were all young adults. Each spent about an hour and a half tapping, pressing, sliding, rotating, and zooming on a numbered grid stuck to the left forearm.

According to recent reports, people press differently and have different skin. A model that was trained on everyone except one volunteer, was then tested on that volunteer. It recognized gestures only about half the time.

According to recent reports, each new user therefore performs a short set of standard taps and gestures first, a calibration that takes just under four minutes. Afterward, the system identified the gesture 92.8 percent of the time and told a gentle press from a hard one 90.2 percent of the time.

Sources indicate that the system also placed a fingertip to within about 0.4 inches (10 millimeters). In other words, the calibration brought a fresh user almost up to the accuracy the system reached on people it had trained on.

Recent findings suggest that ten of the volunteers came back twice more over three months and put the wristband on again. The original calibration still held, at about 91 percent for gestures.

Twelve participants then raced a cursor between targets on a smartwatch display, using their forearm skin as a touchpad. The standard pointing test required them to select each target with a hard two-finger press. The smallest targets were 0.05 inches (1.28 millimeters) across, narrower than a key on a watch keyboard.

The same people did the task on a touchscreen and with a tilt cursor steered by angling the wrist. On the touchscreen they missed 21.7 percent of targets.

With EpiPad they missed 6.5 percent, and they moved between targets faster than with either other method.

“EpiPad outperformed the other two tasks with regard to both error rate and efficiency,” Fu noted.

According to recent reports, the system responded in about 90 milliseconds, within the range of commercial devices. Reading pressure took longer, about half a second. The authors found that most hard presses lasted at least that long anyway.

According to recent reports, in a test on two people, a tight sleeve barely mattered. A loose jacket dropped gesture recognition to 72 percent and pressure detection to 63 percent, because the fabric moves on its own and reflects the radar.

According to recent reports, models calibrated for the index and middle fingers also stumbled when people switched to thumb and index, until they recalibrated for the new pair. Five volunteers who walked slowly while using it kept accuracy near 90 percent.

The prototype is a wristband with a circuit board sticking out, and it still needs a laptop to process the signal.

The authors wrote that custom hardware with more transmitters could let the radar sit lower, to fit thinner watches. Longer studies in daily life, they wrote, would be needed to judge how people take to it.

Xu stated the parts cost less than $10 and could go into smart glasses and other screenless wearables, using “the wearer’s own skin as a full touch surface.”.

Industry observers note that the paper was presented at the UbiComp/ISWC conference in Shanghai in October. The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies.

Latest Update: The rocks beneath forests may hold a hidden key to carbon storage

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research reveals how the weathering of limestone may help forest soils accumulate and preserve carbon from microbial remains.
  • Dead leaves are the obvious source of the carbon in soil.
  • What soil bacteria and fungi leave behind when they die outlasts the plant matter it was built from.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research reveals how the weathering of limestone may help forest soils accumulate and preserve carbon from microbial remains.

Dead leaves are the obvious source of the carbon in soil. About half of soil organic carbon, though, comes from the remains of dead microbes.

What soil bacteria and fungi leave behind when they die outlasts the plant matter it was built from.

In a recent development, A team in China has now tied that microbial carbon to the rock underneath. Forest soils over limestone and dolomite, rocks that dissolve in rainwater, hold more of it than soils over other rock.

At the sites where the rock was dissolving fastest, there was more of it still.

Peilei Hu led the work at the Institute of Subtropical Agriculture, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, with Wei Zhang and Kelin Wang as senior authors.

Co-authors came from CREAF in Barcelona and Aarhus University in Denmark.

The team worked at three scales. There was a reanalysis of forest soils worldwide, a survey of 60 plots in southwest China, and a run of jars on a laboratory bench.

Plants pull carbon out of the air, and some of it reaches the soil as litter and root material.

Microbes eat it, grow, divide and die, and what is left of their bodies is called necromass.

That necromass can last a long time, especially once it sticks to mineral surfaces where other microbes can’t easily reach it.

So two steps decide how much piles up. First, plant carbon has to be turned into microbial bodies.

Then those microbial remains have to resist decomposition.

Soil chemistry governs both steps, and the rock below sets much of the chemistry.

Carbonate rocks underlie more than 15% of the continental land surface and dissolve at least ten times faster than many silicate-bearing rocks.

As they go, they release calcium and raise soil pH.

Studies of carbonate weathering have mostly asked how much carbon dioxide the dissolving rock itself consumes. That left the organic side of the ledger open.

The team started with an existing global database and kept 466 forest topsoil records.

Each one measured total soil organic carbon and amino sugars, the fragments of microbial cell walls that stand in for necromass.

A karst aquifer map sorted the records into 69 over carbonate rock and 397 over other kinds.

Per unit of soil, karst sites held 43.4% more amino sugars than the rest, and 57.6% more organic carbon overall.

According to recent reports, as a share of the carbon present, though, microbial remains were no higher over carbonate rock than anywhere else. Globally, both pools simply ran bigger together.

The field survey in southwest China came out differently.

The work ran across six regions: Nanchuan, Suiyang, Dushan, Huanjiang, Wuming and Longzhou. In each one, the team paired a forest on carbonate rock with a forest on clastic rock and sampled five plots of each.

Industry observers note that the karst forests carry less wood and fewer tree species than their neighbors, on soil that is shallow and patchy. Total soil carbon came out about the same between the pairs.

But the proportion of carbon derived from microbial remains was 19.3% higher in karst soils, and 57.8% more of their amino sugars were bound to mineral surfaces.

To put a number on the weathering itself, the team buried limestone tablets in the karst plots and left them there for a year.

One lay on the soil surface, one sat 4 inches (10 centimeters) down, and one was wedged at the boundary between soil and bedrock. Weighing what each tablet had lost gave a rate.

Those rates were the strongest predictor of microbial carbon in the karst soils, ahead of the microbes’ own numbers and diversity.

Of the combined weight the model gave its predictors, weathering rate accounted for 46.5%, and the abundance of genes for breaking down tough plant compounds another 31.9%.

Recent findings suggest that lignin, the stiff compound that makes wood woody, was scarcer in karst soils and more chemically chewed up. Over non-karst rock, the same analysis turned up climate and plant community instead of weathering.

It has been revealed that field patterns cannot settle which way the arrow points. Microbes help dissolve rock as surely as dissolving rock changes microbes, and the authors say as much.

The laboratory part was built to answer that. The team stirred 4 grams of either limestone powder or quartz sand into 40 grams of karst soil, 54 jars in all.

Each jar was then fed plain water, glucose or glycine, an amino acid.

The glucose and the glycine were built with carbon-13, a heavier form of carbon that can be traced wherever it goes. The jars then sat at 77°F (25°C) for 64 days.

Sources indicate that limestone raised the pH and the calcium available in the soil, as expected. It also shifted which enzymes the microbes made.

They put less into splitting simple sugars and more into attacking tougher material, though that second shift was only marginal.

The labeled carbon is the result that matters.

With limestone in the jar, more of it ended up in microbial remains rather than breathed out as carbon dioxide. The gain was 22% for glucose and 71% for glycine.

For the second step, keeping the necromass, the team separated the calcium in the field soils into four forms and asked which tracked the mineral-bound amino sugars.

Two did: a loosely held, readily exchangeable form, and a form tied up with carbonate minerals themselves.

Calcium can bridge organic matter to mineral surfaces, and carbonate surfaces can take up and bury the remains directly.

Neither bond is permanent on its own, the authors note, but together they put microbial carbon somewhere microbes have trouble getting at it.

That connects the two halves. The same dissolving rock that helps turn plant carbon into microbial bodies also supplies the calcium that keeps those bodies in place.

The global half of the study is forest topsoil only, down to 8 inches (20 centimeters), and 69 karst records against 397 others.

Whether the pattern holds in grassland, farmland or deeper soil is untested. The regional work did not measure leaf litter directly, so plant inputs enter it only through proxies.

And the jar experiment cannot say which part of weathering did the work. Limestone changes pH, calcium and probably nitrogen and phosphorus all at once.

Telling those apart, the authors wrote, needs “longer-term factorial experiments.”.

Crushed rock spread on farmland is already being tested as a way to pull carbon dioxide from the air, and limestone is one of the rocks on the table.

This study does not measure how much carbon that would store, or for how long. What it offers is a mechanism to test.

The rock may add carbon to the soil through the microbes living in it, and not only through the chemistry of its own dissolving.

The full study was published in the journal National Science Review.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Friday, November 27As fall deepens and winter approaches, the wintertime star patterns are reappearing in our evening sky.
  • Look east late tonight to locate the waning gibbous Moon near the border of Gemini and Cancer.
  • Recent findings suggest that sunrise: 6:59 A.M.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Friday, November 27As fall deepens and winter approaches, the wintertime star patterns are reappearing in our evening sky. One is a large asterism called the Winter Hexagon, now fully above the horizon by about 10 P.M. local time. You should be able to spot this shape even with the Moon nearby, as each point in the Winter Hexagon is a bright, well-known star.

Look east late tonight to locate the waning gibbous Moon near the border of Gemini and Cancer. This will help you find the first point in the Hexagon, the pair of stars Castor and Pollux, the heads of Gemini the Twins, glowing just above the Moon at this time. From there, look upward for another bright star in neighboring Auriga — this is Capella, the next point in the Hexagon. From Capella, look left and down just a little to find the V-shaped face of Taurus the Bull, where the bright star Aldebaran shines, marking the next point. Then it’s down to Orion’s bright knee, Rigel, before you drop down and a little left, close to the horizon, to land on Sirius, the brightest star in the sky and the nose of Canis Major. The Hexagon closes out with the luminary of the Little Dog, Procyon.

In a recent development, saturday, November 28Saturn remains a bright naked-eye object all evening, setting around 2 A.M. local time. Around 8 P.M., you’ll find it high in the south, to the left of the Circlet of Pisces and above the body of Cetus the Whale.

Tonight and for the next few nights, Saturn’s strange, two-faced moon Iapetus is skimming north of the planet, making it easier to find. Now glowing at 11th magnitude, it is heading west toward a late December western elongation, when it will shine about a magnitude brighter but sit far from Saturn. Once you’ve got Saturn in your scope, look about 2’ northeast to land on Iapetus. Over the next few nights, it will move westward, reaching inferior conjunction and standing due north of the ringed world by the 30th.

According to recent reports, if you can catch 11th-magnitude Iapetus, you’ll also see four brighter moons: 10th-magnitude Dione, Rhea, and Tethys closer to Saturn; and mid-8th-magnitude Titan, about 3’ to Saturn’s west. The latter is the planet’s largest and brightest moon, easy to spot in any size scope and often even binoculars. If you keep returning each night to track Iapetus, also keep an eye on Titan, which is moving eastward toward the planet and will pass south of Saturn on December 2. Dione, Rhea, and Tethys have smaller orbits and shorter periods, so they move visibly over the course of several hours, frequently swapping places and passing in front of or behind Saturn. For example, Dione disappears behind Saturn’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 12:20 A.M. EST on the 29th (still late on the 28th in time zones farther west).

Sources indicate that sunrise: 7:00 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 9:10 P.M. Moonset: 11:09 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (73%).

Sunday, November 29Have you ever seen your shadow by planetlight? Venus reaches greatest brilliancy at 2 P.M. EST, now shining at magnitude –4.9. Rising nearly three and a half hours before the Sun, Venus will be so bright that it could potentially cast a shadow if you’re in a location with particularly dark skies (Bortle 1 or 2).

Even without perfect viewing conditions, this morning star can’t be missed. By an hour before sunrise, Venus is roughly 25° high in the southeast, blazing just to the lower left of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo. Far to Venus’ lower left, closer to the ground, Mercury stands nearly 5° above the horizon, shining at magnitude –0.7.

Compare the two planets through a telescope. Venus is a 27%-lit crescent, but its disk stretches 40” across. Mercury, by comparison, is much smaller, just 6” across, but its phase is 82%. Now through the first week of December is the best time to catch the solar system’s smallest planet, as it remains bright but appears to sink toward the horizon day by day. By the 5th, Mercury will be less than 2° high an hour before sunrise, making viewing challenging both because of potential obstacles on the horizon as well as the more turbulent layer of air near the ground.

Venus, meanwhile, stays at roughly the same altitude an hour before sunrise all month, its phase growing to nearly 50% lit by the end of the year. Earth’s sister planet will remain prominent in the morning sky through the first half of next year.

It has been revealed that sunrise: 7:01 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 10:25 P.M. Moonset: 11:43 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (62%).

According to recent reports, monday, November 30Venus remains a brilliant and unmissable morning star, but it’s not the only object worth paying attention to before dawn. Leo is hosting a celestial get-together this morning as the Moon joins two planets and the star that sits at the heart of the Lion, just beneath the Sickle asterism.

In a recent development, the waning gibbous Moon is the brightest object here; next brightest is Jupiter, located to the Moon’s upper right and glowing at magnitude –2.2. The gas giant stands nearly side by side with Mars (to Jupiter’s left); the Red Planet is fainter but still a respectable magnitude 0.4. Both planets are slowly growing in brightness and size as they approach opposition early next year. Through a telescope, Jupiter stretches 39” across, offering excellent views of its alternating light and dark cloud bands, and Mars is now 8” wide.

Industry observers note that shining between Mars and the Moon is 1st-magnitude Regulus, often drawn as both the heart of Leo and the base of the Sickle asterism’s handle. The curving backward question mark of stars that forms the Sickle’s blade and the Lion’s head in profile lies above the grouping in the sky before dawn.

Sliding along the ecliptic, the Moon passes 1.2° south of Jupiter at 4 A.M. EST, then 1.1° south of Regulus at 10 A.M. EST and 3° south of Mars at 3 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 7:02 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 11:36 P.M. Moonset: 12:11 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (51%).

Tuesday, December 1Last Quarter Moon occurs at 1:09 A.M. EST. A few hours later, asteroid 2 Pallas reaches a stationary point at 7 A.M. EST. Located in Cetus, it is visible all evening, setting around 1 A.M. local time. It stands highest around 8 P.M., when it’s roughly 30° above the southern horizon, about 4.2° southeast of 2nd-magnitude Diphda (Beta [β] Ceti).

Glowing at magnitude 9.0, Pallas is easy to find with a small scope. It sits near a neat triangle of 5th- to 6th-magnitude stars, which lie about 1.5° southwest of the asteroid and act as a great reference point to find it tonight. Pallas is 1° east of the easternmost star. Previously, Pallas was closing on that star, moving westward. But after tonight, it will turn and move slowly eastward again, pulling away from the little triangle night by night.

Drop about 5° south of this region for an added treat: 8th-magnitude globular cluster NGC 288, just over the celestial border in Sculptor. Spanning about 13’, this ancient ball of stars lies nearly 49,000 light-years away. It’s also near another deep-sky target, the 7th-magnitude galaxy NGC 253. Often called the Silver Coin or Sculptor Galaxy, this stunning edge-on spiral lies about 1.7° northwest of NGC 288 and can be viewed together with the cluster in wide-field instruments such as binoculars or finder scopes.

Visible in the evening sky, Vesta sits more than 40° above the southern horizon around 7 P.M. local time. Previously moving retrograde, or westward, it will now begin moving prograde, or eastward, against the background stars.

Recent findings suggest that this month Vesta is located roughly halfway between bright Saturn to its northwest and magnitude 3.6 Theta (θ) Ceti to its southeast. Saturn is impossible to miss, as it’s the brightest object in this region of the sky. To locate 7th-magnitude Vesta, find Saturn early in the evening and slide about 8.1° east-southeast to land on the main-belt world. There aren’t a lot of background stars in the immediate vicinity, so try to match your view to the star chart above to locate the asteroid in your eyepiece. Because it’s moving slowly, you’ll need to come back every night or two to check out the view and note the light that’s shifted position — that’s Vesta.

Thursday, December 3Look north a few hours after sunset to find the W-shaped star pattern of Cassiopeia on her head, looking more like the letter M as this circumpolar constellation swings above the North Celestial Pole. Just 1.9° northwest of Navi (Gamma [γ] Cassiopeiae), the midpoint of the M (or W), is a lovely open cluster cataloged as NGC 225 and known as the Sailboat Cluster.

Longtime Astronomy contributor Rod Pommier gave the cluster its nickname because he saw an arc of stars within the cluster that looked to him like the sail of a boat catching the wind, connected to a straight line of stars forming the mast and another eight stars outlining the vessel itself. The stars of the cluster are roughly 2,100 light-years distant, and this grouping was discovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783.

For added visual interest, the cluster is set against a complex of dark nebulae made of dust, which block the starlight behind them.

Cataloged as NGC 7426, this 13th-magnitude stellar smudge sits close to a lovely pair of contrasting stars, making finding it a rewarding sight for all: While you do need a larger scope to track down the galaxy, the stars are visible even through smaller instruments, offering something for everyone.

Every fall and winter evening, tens of thousands of American crows fly to the same spot to sleep, and scientists can only guess why they do it

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • American crows gather in huge winter roosts, possibly for protection, warmth, access to food and opportunities to share information.
  • On fall and winter evenings, American crows leave their daytime haunts and fly to shared sleeping sites called roosts.
  • Some roosts hold fewer than 100 crows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American crows gather in huge winter roosts, possibly for protection, warmth, access to food and opportunities to share information.

On fall and winter evenings, American crows leave their daytime haunts and fly to shared sleeping sites called roosts.

Some roosts hold fewer than 100 crows. Others hold hundreds of thousands, or even more than a million. Roosts that number in the tens of thousands are common.

Dr. Kevin J. McGowan of the Cornell Lab of Ornithology addressed the question in a guide last updated in 2010. Why crows do it is “largely a matter of conjecture,” he wrote, listing four hypotheses.

It has been revealed that american crows often live in family groups made up of a breeding pair and offspring from the previous two years. The whole family helps raise the young.

Their diet runs from grains, seeds, fruits and insects to small animals, carrion and garbage. They are also known for solving problems and finding unusual food sources.

Recent findings suggest that partners in Flight estimates the species’ global breeding population at 28 million. Numbers declined slightly between 1966 and 2019, according to the North American Breeding Bird Survey.

Industry observers note that during the nesting season, most breeding crows sleep on their own territories. Afterward they join the roosts.

“It appears that all crows will join winter roosts, even territorial breeding crows,” he wrote.

Non-breeding crows may stay on the home territory, wander between foraging flocks or leave the area for months.

Roost numbers peak in winter and fall away near the start of the breeding season, usually in March.

An hour or two before full darkness, crows collect in an area away from the final roost. There they spend their time calling, chasing and fighting.

Recent findings suggest that groups from several of these congregation areas may merge at one staging area. At dark, the main body moves to the roost itself.

That final site can be a single dense woodlot or a spread of many suitable trees.

A 1972 report put one roost at Fort Cobb, Oklahoma, at more than two million crows.

It has been revealed that the first hypothesis is about the site. Crows may gather because one spot offers good shelter, protection from predators or suitable trees.

The guide compares that kind of roost to a crowded hotel, where the guests share a building but do not really interact.

In a recent development, the second idea is safety in numbers. Large owls are the predators crows fear most, and a crow in a group may be safer than one alone.

“Owls probably are regular attendants at crow roosts,” he added.

Crows also work together to harass or drive off predators, a behavior called mobbing.

Recent findings suggest that under the third hypothesis, the roost works as an information center. A hungry crow could watch for well-fed arrivals in the evening.

It could then trace their flight paths back, or follow them at dawn, to a rich food source.

Recent findings suggest that the fourth is called patch-sitting. Roosts may form close to food that is reliable and impossible to defend.

Landfills, commercial composting facilities and certain farm fields all qualify. Sleeping nearby gives the crows breakfast before they disperse.

A 1997 study in The Auk, led by Donald F. Caccamise, followed color-marked and radio-tagged crows.

By day, most stayed faithful to their group territory all year. They frequently left it to forage up to 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) away.

Recent findings suggest that at night they roosted either at home or at a large roost about 11 miles (18 kilometers) away, next to a landfill. They slept on their territories 87 percent of the time in spring and 42 percent in winter.

Each crow reached the communal roost on its own, not with its group.

Group cohesion was high on territories. The team tied keeping a territory to holding a breeding site.

The team linked communal roosting to likely foraging benefits. Those count most in winter, when food on a territory is scarcest.

In a recent development, crows have gathered in large fall and winter roosts “for as long as there have been crows,” according to McGowan. By 2010, the roost at Auburn, New York, was downtown.

In a recent development, A large roost was recorded near that town in 1911-12. In the winter of 1932-33, about 25,000 crows slept 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) south of it.

Hunting is one possible reason. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act was extended to crows in 1972, and firing a gun inside city limits is prohibited.

Cities are also often 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit (about 3 to 6 degrees Celsius) warmer than the surrounding countryside. Great horned owls should be scarcer in urban areas.

According to recent reports, streetlights and parking lot lights may help crows spot a threat such as an owl and find a fresh perch at night. Large old trees in parks and cemeteries may be especially attractive for roosting.

The information was obtained from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology’s crow FAQ.

The light left behind traces NII, though it can still contain some Hα.

#170125. Physicists break through a major speed barrier in quantum computing

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (930 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Physicists break through a major speed barrier in quantum computing

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicists achieved exceptionally fast and accurate quantum operations by correcting an overlooked source of error in superconducting qubits.
  • Inside a quantum computer, speed and accuracy are supposed to pull against each other.
  • Flip a quantum bit faster and you have to hit it harder, and a hard hit tends to knock it into states it was never meant to occupy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicists achieved exceptionally fast and accurate quantum operations by correcting an overlooked source of error in superconducting qubits.

Inside a quantum computer, speed and accuracy are supposed to pull against each other.

Flip a quantum bit faster and you have to hit it harder, and a hard hit tends to knock it into states it was never meant to occupy.

A team in Germany has now flipped a qubit in 6.8 nanoseconds and got it right more than 99.98% of the time.

Such operations usually take several tens of nanoseconds, and light travels only about 6.5 feet (2 meters) in 6.8 of them.

The gain came from an error that earlier correction methods had overlooked, and it was measured on a single isolated qubit, so larger processors are still untested.

A qubit holds its fragile quantum state for only a limited time.

Every basic operation, or gate, has to fit inside that window, and complex algorithms and error correction need a great many of them.

So the shorter each gate, the more useful work a quantum computer can do before its qubits forget.

The catch is physics. A gate on a superconducting qubit is a pulse of microwaves, and a shorter pulse has to be stronger to do the same job.

Physicists at Forschungszentrum Jülich, working with colleagues at RWTH Aachen University and the University of Cologne, set out to find how far that could be pushed.

Yuan Gao and Rami Barends ran the experiments at the Institute for Functional Quantum Systems, and Felix Motzoi’s group at the Institute for Quantum Control supplied the theory.

Sources indicate that the type of superconducting qubit used in this study isn’t a true two-state system. It has a ladder of energy levels, and a computer uses only the bottom two.

Recent findings suggest that think of an elevator meant to run between the ground floor and the first floor. Push it too hard and it overshoots.

Engineers have known since 2009 that a strong pulse can carry a qubit one level too far.

In a recent development, the standard fix, a pulse-shaping method called DRAG, was built to stop that. Motzoi was a co-author of the 2009 paper that introduced it.

What the newly introduced work showed is that a strong, fast pulse can also lift the qubit two levels at once.

Those double jumps come from absorbing two packets of microwave energy together, and at very short gate times they turned out to be the main source of error.

They’re also hard to undo, the authors wrote, because a qubit stuck on a high level can stay there through many steps and corrupt error correction.

The team’s solution, called R2D, applies the DRAG correction twice to suppress the microwave frequencies that cause the qubit to jump two energy levels at once.

The researchers adjusted just three parameters, testing the qubit repeatedly to find the optimal settings.

The team also needed a new way to measure the result, because leakage this small is hard to see.

So they built a sequence that repeats a gate hundreds of times with a twist of phase between repeats, which makes the stray population pile up instead of washing out.

With it, they could measure leakage down to about one part in a million, where the standard method starts to blur.

The new sequence gave a clear leakage signal within 400 operations, where the standard method needed 800 gates for a weaker one.

Compared with the standard DRAG correction on its own, the fresh pulse shape cut leakage by more than a factor of 20 at the same gate length.

The researchers ran the test on a single transmon qubit, built at Jülich’s Helmholtz Nano Facility and run at 5.323 gigahertz.

They tried pulses from 6.6 to 9 nanoseconds long, with 1 nanosecond of padding after each to absorb distortion.

Shorter pulses made the math unstable, and longer ones overflowed the memory of the control electronics.

At 6.8 nanoseconds, the two basic gates, a full flip of the qubit and a half flip, came out with accuracies of 99.981% and 99.989%.

Industry observers note that the chance of the qubit escaping to a higher level stayed below 0.002% per gate. So the researchers achieved exceptionally high accuracy even at this short gate time.

Pushed to 6.6 nanoseconds, leakage to the third level took over, which the team’s simulation had predicted.

For the full flip, control error also grew as pulses got shorter, which the team attributed to distortion of the microwave pulse on its way in.

Most of the remaining error came from decoherence, the qubit losing its state on its own, at about one part in 10,000 per gate.

The authors called the pulse strength, measured against the spacing of the qubit’s levels, a record for single-qubit gates on superconducting hardware.

Sources indicate that everything here happened on one qubit sitting by itself. Whether the pulse shape works as well inside a larger processor, and during gates that act on two qubits at once, hasn’t been tested.

The authors wrote that the same approach should carry over to two-qubit gates and to other kinds of qubits.

The next step is the hardware. With longer-lived qubits and a tighter handle on pulse distortion, the team wrote, the method could reach gates that are right 99.999% of the time.

That is one more nine than this experiment managed.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#170123. The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Industry observers note that ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a fresh scale measuring masculinity.
  • Recent findings suggest that for almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a fresh scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

Recent findings suggest that for almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” says Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health challenges — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

The first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

Sources indicate that that thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”.

According to recent reports, the higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”.

Industry observers note that yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson says. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Industry observers note that englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

According to recent reports, he and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

According to recent reports, but the study also highlighted that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Recent findings suggest that then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their latest masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work reveals. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”.

Industry observers note that “I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott claims. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”.

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he claims. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”.

According to recent reports, fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher indicates. “And he’s been struggling.”.

Sources indicate that perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher indicates. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales at the moment in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a newly introduced masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

Movember Institute of Men’s Health.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher says. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

According to recent reports, fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he states.

Industry observers note that A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”.

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, states psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a latest masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Recent findings suggest that theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”.

Such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher states. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Sources indicate that reconciliation may be possible, Addis says. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

However the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”.

#170122. AI chatbots may be recommending medications for the wrong reasons

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1002 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

AI chatbots may be recommending medications for the wrong reasons

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers found that leading AI chatbots disproportionately recommend brand-name medications, potentially driving up prescription drug costs.
  • Ask a chatbot which version of a blood pressure pill to take, and you might expect it to weigh the options the way a pharmacist would.
  • It was usually a brand-name drug with a significant online footprint, and usually not the one doctors prescribe most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers found that leading AI chatbots disproportionately recommend brand-name medications, potentially driving up prescription drug costs.

Ask a chatbot which version of a blood pressure pill to take, and you might expect it to weigh the options the way a pharmacist would. Instead, five leading AI models kept naming the same product.

It was usually a brand-name drug with a significant online footprint, and usually not the one doctors prescribe most.

Following those recommendations would raise U.S. drug purchase costs by tens of millions of dollars a year, the researchers estimated.

Daiju Ueda of Osaka Metropolitan University led the study with colleagues at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

His team tested the models on made-up patients, not real prescriptions, so the cost figure is a projection rather than a bill anyone has paid.

The team wrote 177,120 short patient scenarios. Each named a common disease and the active ingredient a doctor planned to prescribe, such as amlodipine for high blood pressure.

Each also described the patient by age, sex, race or ethnicity, LGBTQ+ identity and income, with any of those details sometimes left out.

The scenarios covered 123 disease and drug pairs, each run through 1,440 patient profiles.

Five AI models answered every scenario: GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Flash, Llama 4 and MedGemma.

Each was asked to list up to three FDA-approved products by name, in order of preference. Four physicians then checked more than 883,000 answers against the FDA’s drug registries.

Recent findings suggest that on average, 5.5 approved products existed for each ingredient. Yet across the disease and drug pairs, the most favored product accounted for an average of 97.5% of first-choice picks.

The alternatives, in other words, almost never came up first.

Sources indicate that pooling the five models together, one product drew more than 90% of first choices in 96 of the 123 pairs. The models also agreed with one another, almost all of the time, on which product that was.

The team then compared those picks with what Americans are actually dispensed, using the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, a national survey of prescription use, for 2019 through 2023.

The most commonly prescribed product matched a model’s first choice in only 29.7% of cases, and landed anywhere in its top three in 58.8%.

Weighted by how many prescriptions each drug accounts for, the first-choice match fell to 17%. So, the models’ preferred product was usually not the version most commonly prescribed.

Prices came from the federal National Average Drug Acquisition Cost database, which tracks what retail pharmacies pay.

Complete pricing existed for 51 of the ingredients, and for 38 of those the models’ preferred products cost more than the ones in real use.

More often than not, then, the models leaned toward the pricier option.

The team then asked what would happen if doctors prescribed exactly as the models recommended, across those 51 ingredients, at current prescription volumes.

Industry observers note that “We found that annual acquisition costs would increase by approximately US$55.6 million,” Ueda remarked. “This represents a 1,019% increase in the cost of purchasing these prescriptions.”.

Industry observers note that the $55.6 million covers only the 51 ingredients with full price data. It also assumes a pharmacy fills exactly what the model names, with no generic substitution at the counter.

According to recent reports, what made a product the favorite? Being the original brand-name version mattered most. An originator product had about 20 times the odds of being recommended over a generic with the same ingredient.

“The recommendations were mostly for brand-name drugs, those highly visible in Google searches, and treatments with dedicated Wikipedia pages,” Ueda said.

A product with its own Wikipedia page had three times the odds of being named, and more Google search results raised the odds too. Products approved more recently, and products that doctors prescribe more often in practice, were recommended less. Heavier advertising spending by the manufacturer slightly lowered the odds.

Industry observers note that not every answer was a product a pharmacist could fill. Between 12.4% and 14.7% of each model’s recommendations failed a regulatory check. In nearly all of those cases, the model had named a product that was once FDA-approved but is no longer sold. GPT-5.4 had the lowest rate and Claude Sonnet 4.6 the highest.

Industry observers note that the patient’s description changed those odds. Scenarios describing a Black patient had 1.64 times the odds of drawing a regulatory miss, compared with scenarios that left race unstated. For an Asian patient the figure was 1.16 times.

The authors wrote that such outputs were a minority and do not necessarily mean a clinically wrong choice. But any evaluation of these tools, they added, should report its results by patient group.

When the team rewrote the prompt to ask for the lowest-cost or generic option, the chatbots did shift.

The top pick changed in 63% of comparisons under the lowest-cost prompt and 78% under the generic prompt, and when it changed, it usually moved to a generic.

But the answers stayed just as concentrated, with a single product still taking 93% to 98% of first choices under each latest prompt.

The scenarios were synthetic, and the authors wrote that they shouldn’t be read as a measure of how people actually prescribe.

The researchers also stopped at the recommendation and left out rare diseases and complicated cases.

The study didn’t follow what a doctor, an insurer or a pharmacist would do next. Whether a chatbot’s pick changes what a patient finally receives is the open question.

The authors wrote that the next studies need realistic clinical scenarios, tests of whether lower-cost prompts actually work, and a look at how doctors use these AI assistants.

“Combining AI systems with trusted drug information sources and human oversight may help support more appropriate medication choices,” Ueda said.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 26: Thanksgiving turkey in the sky.

The Moon-free window for observing Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS reopens tonight, the same day the comet reaches perihelion, the closest point to the Sun in its 21½-year orbit. It has been a fairly stable 10th to 11th magnitude, and although it has no appreciable tail, the nucleus’ green glow has been notable in recent astrophotos.

It has been revealed that you’ll find Hartley-IRAS in the west a few hours after sunset. Around 7 P.M. local time it is still 30° high, well above the turbulent air near the ground that can muddy astronomical views. Tonight the comet is in western Sagitta, about 6.3° north-northeast of 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Aquilae. Even a small (4-inch) scope will net you a view, but larger apertures will show more detail around the nucleus, allowing you to look for features such as a sharpened southern flank as it flies into the solar headwind.

While you’re in this region, make sure to sweep just 2.1° northeast of the comet’s location to spot the famous Coathanger asterism in Vulpecula. This 1°-long grouping of stars looks just like its namesake, with the hook on the southern side of the hanger’s arms.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise: 6:59 A.M.Sunset: 4:36 P.M.Moonrise: 7:53 P.M.Moonset: 10:26 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.
