💡 Key Takeaways
  • QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines.
  • QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website.
  • A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them.

A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

Sources indicate that from a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real tech giant.

Recent findings suggest that you think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

It has been revealed that A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

In a recent development, you may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

Sources indicate that if anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

According to recent reports, that does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

It has been revealed that the FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

In a recent development, do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

According to recent reports, if the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

In a recent development, we call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

In a recent development, most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the tech giant, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car tech giant, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

In a recent development, first, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

If you scanned a suspicious code:.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car manufacturer, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

At a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

Sources indicate that no. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

Sources indicate that the goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:.

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

It has been revealed that scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

It has been revealed that inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

It has been revealed that before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

Whether you're a seasoned hiker or an it-girl who just wants to get in on the canvas tote trend, read on for the best ways to save at L.L.Bean this Black Friday.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
  • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
  • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

In a recent development, hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

Recent findings suggest that that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an vital part of it.”.

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” noted Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley noted that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley noted. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

A spokesperson for Roblox noted in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place people under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson mentioned. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She noted Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

Industry observers note that “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles mentioned. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

It has been revealed that wander is a vacation rental organization which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. Upcoming destinations keep popping up!

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

That’s highly competitive in any hotel market for two rooms and the x-factor comes in the form of privacy, full on kitchens, gym facilities, often and a pool or entertainment area and laundry too.

Latest Update: This Cruise Proves the Congo is No Heart of Darkness—Or Viral Fad

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward.
  • According to recent reports, the idea could be mentioned to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory.
  • Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward. Few places exert quite this pull like the Congo Basin, a thick block of forest and rivers covering much of Central Africa, home to some 150 ethnic groups, and a raft of extraordinary biodiversity. Despite its size and its importance as a counterbalance to climate change, the region endures a dearth of scientific research funding and conservation efforts. Roughly the size of India, it has inspired and vexed many visitors (even those who might otherwise have claimed to have conquered it).

A floating village in the Congo River Basin.

According to recent reports, the idea could be mentioned to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory. The Welsh explorer Henry Morton Stanley, the first to leave a detailed record of his journey across the Basin, claimed that even after a three-year trek (1874-77) it remained “a region of fable and mystery.” That was exactly the mix sought by Polish sailor Józef Korzeniowski, who, as a boy, looked at the map of Africa, then a white space, and “declared that some day I would go there.” Eventually, and not long after Stanley, he did, and with the captaincy of a steamboat on the Congo River, was tasked with collecting one Mr. Klein, an upcountry agent employed by the brutal Belgian trading firm. Korzeniowski was horrified by what he saw along the river—colonization and resource extraction at its cruelest and bloodiest—calling it “the vilest scramble for loot that ever disfigured the history of human conscience and geographical exploration.” Later, Józef Korzeniowski became Joseph Conrad, Mr. Klein became Mr. Kurtz, and the rest is literary history.

Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”.

Sources indicate that the latest journeyman to apply themself to the region is another Welshman, Ash Dykes, whose TikTok videos of his journey paddling down the Sangha River (a tributary of the mighty Congo River) have received millions of views. By mid-October, Dykes, who calls himself an extreme athlete, was midway through the 400 miles he hoped to cover. His videos—the anxiety and speculation of his preparation; the amplification of the danger en route—are over-exaggerated, designed to amuse his audience; they are spectacle. Looking bewildered in his state-of-the-art inflatable boat, Dykes is most often met by competent, unaffected locals, paddling their wooden pirogues with balletic grace. And brave though Dykes certainly is, most of what he has accomplished—attending a hunt with the Ba’aka people, seeing the forest elephants in Dzanga Baï, or tracking Western lowland gorillas—can be done by just about anyone.

The Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions, is the basin's only passenger cruise.

I, too, was one enchanted by the inscrutability of the Congo Basin, and I dreamt of one day traveling along its rivers and into its forests; in my mind’s eye, I envisioned dusk slipping into night, to the rhythm of a pounding drumbeat. Not long ago, I departed Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, aboard the Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions. As the only such passenger vessel in the Congo Basin, the crew of the Ngalessa is accustomed to receiving rarefied looks from the riverbank. But just as often, the ship’s approach was greeted with aplomb, for it was an event in the villages and brought goods, along with community support and news from away.

In a recent development, in comparison to the coarse and crowded daka-dakas—flat-topped river barges, stuffed with goods and spewing black, acrid smoke as they chunter between Kinshasa and Kisangani—those of us onboard the Ngalessa traveled in glorious comfort: air-conditioning, three square meals a day, and private bathrooms. We also had the benefit of our local guides and their familiarity with the languages, customs, and faces up and down the river. This included, in the riverside village of Ngabe, the appearance of an Ejengi, a forest spirit made of palm fronds that danced and spun as a crowd of onlookers sang, drummed, and screamed in delight.

Sources indicate that “Don’t worry,” our guide remarked. “Look at his dusty bare feet!” Elsewhere, we watched an Indigenous Luma woman cut, strip, and chew twigs into a pulp that could be used as medicinal pain relief. On other days, we kayaked through the flooded forests of the Alima River, and traded with fishermen who brought their slim pirogues against our mammoth ship to hand over smoked fish and fruit.

Kayaking through the flooded forests of the Alima River.

Eight days and 600 miles after leaving Brazzaville, we arrived at the outpost of Ouesso on the Sangha River. I journeyed further upon that water by launch boat, into the Central African Republic, and spent days at Sangha Lodge, drinking gin and tonics with local legend Rod Cassidy, an eco-tourism pioneer who has spent years living and working with the local Ba’aka people. It was through him I had the good luck to attend a hunt with those same Ba’aka, and to look on while they divvied up the duiker they snagged in their homemade nets. Afterwards, they whooped and hollered as they carried the meat out and into their village—a feast!

It has been revealed that in the heightened state of travel, there comes occasionally a moment like falling into an empty space and, as two glancing stones can spark a blaze, a light of comprehension is illuminated. Sometimes this moment manifests itself as love, other times as admiration, or confusion. Conrad left the Congo in spiritual, psychological, and physical shock. “Before the Congo, I was a mere animal,” he wrote after his consequential journey. He was changed, as travelers who go forward with their ears and eyes open (to say nothing of their hearts) are changed. Watching the Ba’aka poised in their hunt, ears tilted to the slightest sound, I felt myself see humanity as it had existed since time immemorial. As they laughed and chatted on their success, the women showing their fangs (chipped with rocks as a show of strength), and the men slapping each other on the back, I could barely remember seeing such happiness elsewhere.

The Congo Basin may still be raw and atavistic—great adventures there are still possible—but it is no “heart of darkness” (a title which for Conrad lay not in the location itself, but rather mankind’s ability to exploit and vilify others). What separates it from other places is its independence. It requires protection, yes, but has no need, and few provisions, for any prying visitors; it is not a prize to be conquered. Most incredibly, it remains the home of peoples who have not yet latched themselves to tourism; people who sustain themselves almost wholly from an expanse of forest and the waters that for others can only be the basis of wonder and amazement. And yet, after all the sorrow and misery that colonialism brought to the Congo Basin, the people remain sincere and earnest, and willing to show others the best of their land.

A lone kayaker glides underneath a hazy sky.

Sources indicate that one night, as the Ngalessa drifted northward, from beneath the awning on the ship’s upper deck, I watched a cloud bank clump and darken. Finally, with an incision of lightning, the downpour came, brief but fierce. The sun returned, low in the sky but still warm, and the scent of damp earth rose up. A patter of drumming reached us from somewhere, before being swallowed by the forest. The dinner bell rang, and I thought I never want this trip to end.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs.
  • Barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here.
  • Grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs. Nearly every island has a stretch of powdery sand and improbably blue water, and after a while, the “nice sand, nice water” trope stops registering at all. We’re talking beauty in the transcendental sense—the kind of beauty that makes you feel something. Maybe it’s a crescent of sand more pink than you thought could happen in nature. Maybe it’s a labyrinth of granite boulders spilling into the sea. Or maybe it’s a beach bar so perfectly placed it feels as much a part of the landscape as the sand. Plenty of beaches are picturesque. These are the ones, if you ask us, that are beautiful.

Barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here. The long stretch of blush-pink sand is framed by low vegetation and blissfully few signs of life. There is, almost puzzlingly, a Nobu, which brings a welcome blip of civilization in the form of Japanese-Peruvian cooking, cocktails, and a beach club with cabanas. (Nobu Beach Inn is set to debut in 2027, too.) Book lunch there and a beach transfer in advance—many of the top resorts on Antigua offer this as a day excursion from the other island.

Grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate. An offshore reef keeps the waters agreeably calm for swimming (especially with kids), too. This is one of the Caribbean’s most polished beach destinations, with a concentration of luxury resorts, watersports operators and restaurants that make a choose-your-own adventure beach day a pretty seamless affair. Public access points are plentiful and free, so you needn’t be staying at one of the grand hotels to enjoy the view. (Although you should.).

The kind of place that castaway dreams are made of, Little Bay is a tiny crescent of sand tucked beneath towering limestone cliffs. No beach club, no cabanas, no infrastructure, no fuss. It’s accessible by boat from neighboring Crocus Bay, or, if you’re feeling adventurous, by rope down the rock face. Bring water, a picnic and all your gear—there’s fantastic snorkeling here.

It has been revealed that A mile-long horseshoe of white sand with clear, shallow water, Flamenco Beach is more than worth the ferry over from mainland Puerto Rico. It also has an unusual bit of history: two abandoned United States military tanks, left behind after the Navy used Culebra for training exercises, now sit near the shore, covered in colorful graffiti. We aren’t usually proponents of littering, but the counterpoint of natural beauty with human history is part of what makes this beach so unforgettable.

Sources indicate that definitely the most photographed beach in the U.S. Virgin Islands and probably the most photographed beach in the Caribbean, Trunk Bay never disappoints. From the access road, you see a sweep of white sand stretching out, with impossibly turquoise waters and a small offshore cay that seems placed for composition. It’s part of Virgin Islands National Park, so the infrastructure covers all the stuff you need—snack bar, restrooms, showers and snorkel rentals. The main attraction is the underwater snorkeling trail, where submerged markers introduce visitors to the coral reef and its inhabitants.

If you want swanky French beach clubs, head over to Saint-Jean, because Saline is St. Barth’s at its most elemental. The sand is broad and soft, the dunes rolling, and the sea open, with no beach clubs or hotels or influencers interrupting your view. Getting there requires a short walk over the dunes from the parking lot, which helps preserve the feeling that you’re leaving the chi-chi side of the island behind.

It has been revealed that there are beautiful beaches, and then there are the Baths, a landscape so distinctive it feels like you’ve left the Caribbean, and perhaps earth entirely. The beach is home to a collection of enormous granite boulders, some as large as houses, all tumbled together to create something totally unique. Between them are hidden grottoes, tidal pools and narrow passages—making this as much a playground as it is a beach. Bring sturdy water shoes and expect to do some scrambling.

The longest beach on its island, this elegant crescent sits directly on the Tropic of Cancer. It’s relatively remote and unspoiled by Bahamian standards, making it a true bucket list destination for beach snobs. It’s about a 30-minute drive from George Town on Great Exuma (where the airport is), across the bridge to Little Exuma. There are no proper facilities, so pack what you need. There are Aman, Rosewood and Bulgari resorts debuting here in the years to come—so visit now for serious “I've been coming here since” bragging rights.

A hidden gem by any standard, Sandy Island is a miniature, uninhabited coral cay located just off the west coast of Carriacou, Grenada’s sister island. There are no hotels or roads, and the whole appeal is the rugged simplicity of arriving by boat, dropping anchor and spending an afternoon doing basically nothing except enjoying the elements. The island is part of a protected marine park, making it a fantastic spot for snorkeling with colorful reef fish, turtles and octopi.

The rest of the world is finally catching up with what the diving scene has known for years—No Name Beach is one of the most pristine, stunning stretches of sand anywhere in the Caribbean. It’s located on the tiny island of Klein Bonaire (“Little Bonaire”) just offshore of mainland Bonaire, and is part of Bonaire National Marine Park, meaning development is off the table. There aren’t any restaurants, bathrooms, or beach bars, but there are water taxis from Kralendijk. Bring food and water, your own snorkel gear, and prepare to be blown away by the untouched Caribbean at its finest.

While Bávaro Beach proper is about 5 miles long, it connects seamlessly with adjoining beaches Arena Blanca and Arena Gorda—so, depending on who’s counting, actually comes in at closer to 30 miles of uninterrupted shoreline. This is the beach that initially spurred Punta Cana’s resort boom, with coconut palms fringing the white sand, a barrier reef keeping the waters tranquil, and enough space for everyone to stretch out and (pretty much) never feel crowded. If you head toward El Cortecito or Los Corales, you’ll find beach bars where the party never stops. On a beach this beautiful, why would it?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the latest changes.

It has been revealed that the changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

But what about the redemption of points?

According to recent reports, well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Industry observers note that previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the upcoming version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in Newly introduced York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

In a recent development, if I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive….

In a recent development, yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

Industry observers note that A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

In a recent development, if Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

It has been revealed that you can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
  • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s newly introduced ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s newly introduced ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., noted, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five newly introduced air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

Industry observers note that they justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it promptly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

According to recent reports, “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

Still, Cruz stated the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization initiative so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., mentioned after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

According to recent reports, for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., mentioned the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not massive on government running things.”.

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

Recent findings suggest that “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

Recent findings suggest that he called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy remarked, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

In a recent development, “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy mentioned. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that the telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford remarked Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

According to recent reports, bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

Sources indicate that A pilot reporting strange lights near Baltimore got an unexpected response from ATC, who casually mentioned there had been alien sightings in the area. The pilot joked that he’d have quite the story to tell his family. 👽✈️#ATC #Aviation #Aliens pic.twitter.com/rtalRieUwH.

#169997. How a Screen-Free Retreat in South Africa’s Cederberg Rewired My Nervous System

How a Screen-Free Retreat in South Africa’s Cederberg Rewired My Nervous System

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1487 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the sun dropped behind craggy peaks, the heat-baked sandstone dissolved into a deep twilight, and the silence thickened until the valley became a dark amphitheater.
  • My phone had lost signal hours earlier, somewhere on the winding, vertiginous drive into this private reserve of over 3,300 acres.
  • Cradled by ancient rock, Weaver’s Nest is a villa for two above the Doring River.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the sun dropped behind craggy peaks, the heat-baked sandstone dissolved into a deep twilight, and the silence thickened until the valley became a dark amphitheater. I had come to Bliss & Stars, an off-grid retreat perched above the Doring River deep in South Africa's Cederberg, for Orion's Odyssey, a program timed to the new moon, when the sky is at its darkest. As we neared midnight, the Milky Way's galactic core rose above the ridge, so dense and richly textured, it looked like the luminous, flowing reflection of the river below.

My phone had lost signal hours earlier, somewhere on the winding, vertiginous drive into this private reserve of over 3,300 acres. Initially, I had found that confronting, until I made peace with what I stood to gain. The eye needs around 20 minutes of true darkness to adjust, and a single glance at a bright screen largely undoes it. Without a signal, I had no reason to look down at it. It was just a camera.

Cradled by ancient rock, Weaver’s Nest is a villa for two above the Doring River.

Sources indicate that that encompassing darkness is what brought Heine Rasmussen, an astronomy and nature guide and science communicator, and his wife Daria, a meditation teacher and somatic practitioner, here. In 2018, they left behind the security of corporate life in Copenhagen for a quest to find the least light-polluted skies. After searching around the world, they found them in the Cederberg, just over four hours north of Cape Town.

They acquired the virtually untouched land in 2019, and first had to construct a rudimentary access road before they could start building the lodge. Everything came in by pickup truck and trailer, and was carried by hand for the last stretch. The chalets were wedged between boulders or into the rock face above the river. More recently, the couple added a villa, bringing the total to six units that can accomodate no more than 10 guests.

Recent findings suggest that on these monthly, stargazing-centered retreats, the nights belong to Heine. After dinner each evening, we gathered on a circular, open-air viewing deck in front of the observatory, where mattresses were laid out so we could lie flat and look straight up. One night Heine led us on what he calls "a little mental space walk," a star meditation designed to unground rather than ground us, during which he recounted the history of the universe. With our eyes closed, we breathed the night in through the nose and out through the mouth while he invited the city's stress to leave with each exhalation, until gravity seemed to loosen its grip and our arms and legs felt as if they might float. Falling asleep, he assured us, was perfectly fine.

After a night of stargazing, morning breathwork and yoga with Daria help put life into perspective.

The Cederberg's sandstone boulders have been sculpted by wind and water over aeons.

Sources indicate that at the 20-inch telescope, one of the largest privately owned in South Africa, he taught us without jargon, finding a nebula and talking our small group through it while we took turns peering into the eyepiece. Guests here range from billionaires seeking quiet to people who come for free on the lodge's bursary program, and all of them arrive curious, looking for purpose, or simply to disconnect from the world they’ve left behind.

Heine's first subject: time. Moonlight, he told us, reaches us about a second after leaving the moon; sunlight about eight minutes after leaving the sun. The two pale patches in the southern sky, the Magellanic Clouds, are satellite galaxies of our own, and their light set out more than 160,000 years ago, when our species was young and still almost entirely in Africa. From there he moved to the iron in our blood and the calcium in our bones, forged in stars that exploded before our sun ever existed. I had heard the stardust line many times in other remote locales but never within the context of physics, explained step by step, or woven into a meditation under a sky like this one.

It has been revealed that daria took care of the mornings, which began with a thick, warm ceremonial cacao, readying the nervous system for what was to follow. I missed my regular wake-up coffee, the richness of the chocolatey cacao not compensating for the familiar kick of caffeine. From there, we headed to our yoga mats in an open-air studio where Daria led us in somatic breathwork, referencing the enormity of the night sky. Her view is that star-studded skies like those the Cederberg reliably delivers do not make daily concerns disappear; they merely change their size, put them into perspective. Much of what she imparts during the morning breathwork sessions is about making room to allow yourself to feel that. Daria works with the stress the body becomes so good at absorbing—shallow breaths and a clenched jaw, in my case. From hysterical laughter to sobs of grief, more surfaced for our small circle than any of us had bargained for.

The Cederberg has some of the darkest skies on earth.

After brunch, we hiked narrow paths where Cape mountain leopard tracks were pressed into the sand and raptors like Verreaux's eagles and rock kestrels caught thermals overhead. We scrambled over the orange sandstone rock, carved into fantastical shapes piled like giant, irregular building blocks, before washing off the dust and dry heat in the Doring River, the water surprisingly cool even though it was the end of summer. In the overhangs we marveled at San rock paintings between 2,000 and 5,000 years old, a collection of sites which Heine and Daria are still discovering on their land. There are more than 2,500 known rock art sites in the wider Cederberg, and whenever I see them I can't help thinking that the people who left their mark here once stood in this same silence, under much the same stars.

Every plant-based meal is consciously plated to nourish body, mind, and spirit.

With so much of the day spent on the move, in silence or alone, meals at the long wooden table in the lodge's open-initiative kitchen became the social high point. With caffeine, refined sugar, meat, and alcohol off the menu, dining still felt indulgent despite being based on vegetables, fruit, and whole grains. Daria has little patience for the guilt and pressure so often associated with clean-eating dogma; in the retreat's cookbook, Eat, Thrive, Repeat, she writes about reaching the point where "appetite becomes information rather than judgment." In practice, that meant buddha bowls, ancient grain salads, roasted vegetables, and sweet treats at brunch like beetroot flapjacks with a miso caramel of dates and coconut oil.

It has been revealed that one night, after hiking into the sunset and a surprise dinner in a cave, Heine gave an informal introduction to one of his passions, astrophotography. I learned how to hold a shutter open long enough to gather light the eye cannot. I stood still in the pitch black with a torch under my chin and came away with a portrait of myself against thousands of stars, the camera collecting photons that had been traveling for centuries, some for millennia, before they reached its sensor.

As you fall asleep, the night sky is framed in floor-to-ceiling glass.

On the final night, the telescope and the table worked in tandem. Dinner with Stars ran to six courses, eaten between turns at the eyepiece, and, read in order, the menu told the life story of the universe much as Heine had been telling it to us since we arrived—from Major Bang, a baked carrot dish, through to The White Dwarf, a wild strawberry dessert named for the small, dense ember a star like our sun leaves behind when it dies. The carbon on my fork was made inside stars that died before our sun existed, scattered into space, swept into the cloud of gas and dust that became our solar system, and pulled from the air, eventually, by the carrots on my plate.

Because it was summer and we had to wait for the sky to turn inky black, nights ended well past midnight. Back in my chalet, on a bed stuffed with horsehair, seaweed, and coconut fiber, I sipped from a flask filled with locally grown rooibos sweetened with wildflower honey before drifting off to sleep. The chalet's floor-to-ceiling windows face east over the river and are free of curtains to encourage waking with the morning light—a gentle but powerful way to reset one's circadian rhythm. When I opened my eyes in the small hours, the night sky filled the glass. I had never seen it framed like that.

Running year-round except July in South Africa's Cederberg, Bliss & Stars hosts intimate, all-inclusive retreats in six off-grid units sleeping a maximum of 10 guests.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that I needed to return to the United States after taking my children to Germany for the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Air France delivered one of the best business class flights I have taken in years on my journey from Paris to New York. The new A350-900 cabin is excellent, but what impressed me most was how well everything came together, from the comfortable seat to the delicious dinner, gracious service, and fast Starlink Wi-Fi.

I shared my first impressions of this flight earlier, calling it the best business class experience in Europe. Having had more time to reflect on it, I stand by that assessment…this flight left very little room for improvement.

Recent findings suggest that I needed to return to the United States after taking my children to Germany for the summer. Flying Blue came through with a last-minute business class award from Basel to Paris to Newly introduced York for 60,000 miles plus €453 in taxes and fees. The timing worked perfectly and I booked this about 36-hour before departure, so saver space can certainly open up via FlyingBlue.

Recent findings suggest that this was a so-called “reverse redeye,” leaving Europe late in the evening and arriving in the United States even later that same evening. That suited my prepares very well, particularly because I had an overnight drive to Pittsburgh ahead of me after landing.

Recent findings suggest that my journey began in Basel with an Air France Hop! flight to Paris. I had time to visit the lounge before my connection and enjoyed a meal there, though I deliberately left room for dinner onboard.

It has been revealed that stepping onboard, I found my seat in 6L. Though approaching 8:00 pm, it was still very light outside.

I first reviewed Air France A350 business class in 2020, flying from Paris to Toronto. I enjoyed that flight very much, but the newer business class cabin represents a substantial improvement.

The business class cabin has 48 seats spread over a front and rear cabin. These seats are based on the Stelia Opera platform and are arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration, with every passenger having direct aisle access and a sliding door to provide additional privacy.

Far more important the gimmicky door was the room for your feet, which I found plentiful. Legroom is 43 inches when the seat is the upright position and it transforms into a bed that is 79 inches long. Seats are 21 inches wide.

Recent findings suggest that there are no personal art vents, but thankfully the cabin was kept very chilly. I also loved the window darkening feature, where the window tinting could be adjusted simply by sliding your finger left or right.

It has been revealed that I found this suite spacious and comfortable whether sitting upright, reclining, or lying down. The cabin looks so sharp. I particularly love the illuminated winged seahorse at each seat…a small detail, but one that gives the cabin an unmistakable Air France identity.

There was plenty of personal storage, and the wireless charging worked well, though there was also USB-C and universal A/C power.

After dinner, I converted my seat into a bed and slept for about four hours.

The Sofitel-branded bedding (duvet, mattress pad, pillow) was excellent, and I found the seat very comfortable for sleeping.

This is one of my favorite business class seats.

Recent findings suggest that air France provided a very attractive amenity kit with an embossed seahorse on the bag. It was lined with red and the contents included:.

The catering was a highlight of this flight. I had eaten in the lounge, but was very glad I saved room for dinner.

Before takeoff, flight attendants offered Champagne and a warm towel, along with the familiar Gavottes savory biscuits.

The full menu (every menu item and ingredient is French except for Coca-Cola):.

Dinner began with an appetizer of pea, lemon, and basil cream accompanied by smoked salmon fillet and raspberry and grapefruit jelly.

A side salad accompanied the starter, though I saved mine until after the main course, as the French do. The bread was delicious.

Sources indicate that I also tried the Quintessence cocktail, an Air France variation on a Negroni. It combined La Quintinye royal red vermouth, bitter Chambéry liqueur, a hint of fig, and ABK6 VSOP Cognac. I enjoyed it very much. It was not nearly as strong as a traditional Negroni, which suited me just fine on this flight.

For my main course, I chose veal with a creamy morel mushroom sauce, spelt risotto, and peas.

Admittedly, the presentation was not going to win any awards…yes, it looked like vomit. But it tasted delicious and I would happily order it again. I enjoyed a delicious glass of Chateau D’Arsac wine, which was so good.

According to recent reports, A cheese course followed, then dessert. I enjoyed both ice cream and a crispy hazelnut tart, accompanied by hot chocolate.

This was a substantial supper and a very satisfying one.

About an hour before landing, flight attendants served a light meal of shrimp with a pickled cucumber salad.

In a recent development, it was excellent and just the right amount of food after the large dinner. I had two espressos with it, which helped prepare me for the late night ahead.

Industry observers note that the entertainment system included a tail camera, which I particularly enjoyed during our departure from Paris (though not the fire that seemed to be burning near CDG). It was a gorgeous evening, and watching the aircraft leave Charles de Gaulle was a lovely way to begin the flight.

I did not watch any movies or TV on this flight, but there was large selection of movies, TV indicates, games, and music.

Noise-cancelling headphones were provided, though you can also connect your own Bluetooth device.

Fast, free Starlink internet was available onboard. The connection worked from gate to gate and felt much like using the internet on the ground. I did not have any essential work to complete on this flight, but I appreciated being able to connect onboard. Starlink increasingly influences which flights I book. Air France already gives me plenty of reasons to choose it, but reliable internet makes the proposition even more attractive, especially for a daytime westbound journey when I might otherwise spend several hours working.

The Air France A350 has three lavatories in business class: one I the front (though typically reserved for crew use) and two in between the front and rear cabin.

Service was warm and attentive throughout the flight. I was even addressed by surname.

I have heard plenty of complaints over the years about service on Air France, but my own experiences have been very positive. This crew continued that pattern and the great service complemented the rest of the experience. I enjoyed a delicious meal, slept comfortably, and felt well cared for throughout the journey.

The new seat deserves attention, but a cabin can only do so much without a good crew in terms of leaving a lasting positive impression. On this flight, Air France delivered both.

We landed on time at JFK, and I quickly cleared immigration using Global Entry. The late arrival had been part of the appeal when booking, and the flight delivered exactly what I had hoped for: an enjoyable evening onboard, a few hours of rest, and an on-time arrival in Upcoming York.

Then it was time to collect a rental car and begin my overnight drive to Pittsburgh….

This was a tremendous flight on Air France…I have no complaints at all about anything.

I liked the older A350 business class product when I flew it in 2020, but the newer seat is a considerable improvement. Pair that with excellent bedding, delicious food, and a gracious crew, then add Starlink, and I struggle to identify much that I would change. Cappuccinos maybe that are not powdered?

The lack of individual air vents remains a drawback, though the comfortable cabin temperature thankfully meant it did not interfere with my sleep on this flight.

Recent findings suggest that air France reminded me how enjoyable a transatlantic business class flight can be when the airline gets the details right. I would happily book this product again and would go out of my way to find it.

Passengers eventually continued to Chicago later Wednesday.

As we celebrate Thanksgiving in the USA, that is something to appreciate.

What’s more festive than tucking into a fancy steak dinner on Christmas? Holiday specials at iconic steakhouse Quality Eats include the Après Ski Sangria, featuring red wine, mulling spices and winter citrus; Home Alone, with Angel’s Envy Bourbon, cinnamon and house spruce bitters; and Quality Nog, with Bacardi Ocho, Cognac and homemade spiced nog. Pair any of them with a dry-aged tomahawk ribsteak and 28-Day dry-aged porterhouse served with tableside truffle service.

Rooted in the vibrant and inclusive spirit of Harlem, Red Rooster Harlem is inspired by the neighborhood’s African American, Southern, and Caribbean culinary influences with exciting dishes like its signature Yardbird fried chicken, cornbread and gravy, shrimp and grits, oxtail meatloaf, and more.

At Le Crocodile, the cozy French bistro inside Williamsburg’s Wythe Hotel, celebrate Christmas Day with a special prix fixe menu. Choose from four two-hour seatings available at 11:30 AM, 1:30 PM, 3:30 PM, and 5:30 PM, with an optional wine pairing.

Recent findings suggest that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

In a recent development, but supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

Several senators leaving the meeting mentioned the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

Recent findings suggest that that was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the newly introduced people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she mentioned.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday noted at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

It has been revealed that but there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., mentioned Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

In a recent development, several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

Sources indicate that that included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

In a recent development, “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he mentioned. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

Sources indicate that “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he mentioned. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

Recent findings suggest that sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but noted, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he mentioned. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for fresh leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Industry observers note that senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

In a recent development, “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., remarked, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

Latest Update: Giving Thanks When America Feels Like The Last Days Of Narnia

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this Thanksgiving, I keep thinking about the last days of Narnia.
  • Recent findings suggest that in The Last Battle, an ape named Shift dresses a donkey in a lion’s skin and persuades the Narnians that Aslan has returned.
  • The deception works because the Narnians want to be faithful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this Thanksgiving, I keep thinking about the last days of Narnia. Not because I believe the world is ending, but because C.S. Lewis understood how easily faith can be exploited by those seeking power…and how difficult it becomes to see clearly when we are frightened or angry.

Recent findings suggest that in The Last Battle, an ape named Shift dresses a donkey in a lion’s skin and persuades the Narnians that Aslan has returned. Shift then speaks for him, demanding obedience and using their love for Aslan to advance his own interests.

The deception works because the Narnians want to be faithful. They have difficulty believing that someone invoking Aslan could be asking them to betray everything Aslan represents.

I find that painfully familiar when I watch Christians excuse conduct in Donald Trump that they would rightly condemn in almost anyone else. Once defending a leader becomes a religious obligation, we have given him something that never belonged to him.

The lion’s skin does not make the donkey Aslan. Invoking Christianity does not make a political demand Christian.

That warning applies to me too. Seeing another person’s hypocrisy does not excuse my own contempt. Being right about a political failure does not make every word I write about it righteous.

According to recent reports, I can become so occupied with what is wrong that I stop noticing what God has given me. I can begin to enjoy indignation. That is a dangerous habit for anyone, particularly someone who writes for a living.

It has been revealed that scripture takes ingratitude seriously. In Romans 1:21, Paul describes people who knew God but neither honored Him as God nor gave thanks. Ingratitude accompanies their descent into darkened thinking and idolatry. And in Ephesians 5:3–4, Paul places thanksgiving where corrupt speech ought to be displaced. Gratitude is part of how we resist sin.

Giving thanks reminds me that I am a recipient of mercy. I have no grounds to treat another person as beyond its reach.

According to recent reports, I remain grateful to be an American. I will continue to criticize our government when I believe it deserves criticism, and I will continue to pray for those who govern us, including President Trump.

But my allegiance belongs to the Kingdom of Heaven and to Jesus Christ, the King of Kings. No party gets to borrow that allegiance. No president gets to claim it.

It has been revealed that that gives me freedom to acknowledge something good done by someone I oppose and something wrong done by someone I supported. It also means an election cannot deliver everything I hope for or take away everything that matters.

Industry observers note that paul tells Christians to give thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18). I understand that to include circumstances I want to change. Gratitude does not require pretending that injustice is good or that incompetence is harmless.

Today, I am thankful for my wife and children, for the church that has sustained me, my loving and supportive family and friends, and for the extraordinary privilege of traveling through this world and sharing it with you. Most of all, I am thankful that my hope rests with a King whose character does not require excuses.

According to recent reports, lewis understood that Shift did not have the last word. I need to remember that too.
