  • Standing there in the Kyrgyz countryside, being collectively talked out of one of my more impulsive yeses by a busload of surrogate parents, I felt like a teenager being scolded—defiant but also secretly touched that people I had just met cared enough to save me from myself.
  • On my first trip to Uzbekistan, I joined an Intrepid Travel tour and wondered whether I had booked the wrong departure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a grassy field in Don-Aryk, Kyrgyzstan, men on horseback were wrestling over a headless goat carcass. This is kok boru, the country's national sport, sometimes called dead goat polo. The riders violently wrenched the goat from one another's grip, then tore across the field toward a cauldron-size goal. When the game ended, a player invited me to take a victory lap with the goat. I was two weeks into a Smithsonian Journeys trip across five Central Asian countries with a group of mostly retirees. They knew I was genuinely considering his offer, and their reaction was unanimous: Oh, no you won't.

Standing there in the Kyrgyz countryside, being collectively talked out of one of my more impulsive yeses by a busload of surrogate parents, I felt like a teenager being scolded—defiant but also secretly touched that people I had just met cared enough to save me from myself.

On my first trip to Uzbekistan, I joined an Intrepid Travel tour and wondered whether I had booked the wrong departure. Most of the guests were seniors, so I assumed we would have little in common. Then I met Penny, a septuagenarian from Australia who survived a terrorist bombing in Bali that killed three people in her group. Her husband had suffered brain damage and withdrew from the world; Penny kept traveling, even when it meant going alone. We shopped for textiles in Khiva and bonded over meals; by trip's end, whatever distance I'd imagined between us disappeared.

Sources indicate that that first trip changed more than my assumptions about whom I might enjoy traveling with. My own parents struggled with severe depression and agoraphobia, each condition feeding the other as their shared world contracted. Older travelers like Penny highlighted me another way to age: by staying curious, social, active, and engaged with the world.

Sources indicate that I saw that same determination on a Lindblad Expeditions–National Geographic cruise through the Peruvian Amazon. Dan and Kathy, both widowed after 30-year marriages, met online, fell in love, and kept a list of trips to take. Another guest had cared for her husband through terminal brain cancer, then received her own cancer diagnosis. Hardship hadn't blunted their zest for adventure; if anything, it had magnified it.

I was on board and turning that contrast over in my mind when I found out my dad died.

The next few days bled together. Through the blur my fellow travelers indicated up for me—listening when I wanted to talk and giving me space when I didn't. These folks knew firsthand what it meant to have life cleaved into Before and After. Yet here they were, swimming with piranhas, trekking through the jungle, and plotting where to go next. They were living proof that joy could still exist on the other side of tragedy.

According to recent reports, back in Central Asia my fellow travelers who had vetoed my kok boru ride embodied what I'd come to love about traveling with groups of older people. Linda, an 80-year-old retired psychoanalyst, shared my raunchy humor and skittering attention span during tedious museum tours. I suspected Susan, 83, disapproved when she first asked about my tattoos—until she rolled up her sleeve to reveal Betty Boop on her biceps, acquired at 81. She had survived two comas and a stroke, and still posed for photos in fire-engine red lipstick. A red lip is my signature too. This was my kind of woman.

According to recent reports, the whole group was intimidatingly accomplished: pulmonologists, oncologists, former heads of ICUs and surgical departments. Ask for a doctor, and half the bus could raise a hand. They talked passionately about history and architecture. My PhD dad could turn any conversation into a lecture too; I hadn't realized how much I missed that until I was sermonized at dinner. Their adult children came up often: Would they find the right partner? Start a family? Live up to their potential? Beneath all the second-guessing was enormous tenderness.

Traveling with seniors requires patience, of course. Some use canes and walkers, so itineraries are deliberately less demanding. To me, that's a fair trade.

Industry observers note that on a Viking river cruise that sailed this past summer from Bucharest, Romania, to Budapest, my husband and I hit it off with Bob and Jeannie, a couple from Long Island. They peppered us with questions about our work, our four-year-old son, and our life in Minnesota. That curiosity touched a nerve. My mother, who has dementia and lives with us, no longer asks about my job, my kid, or anything else. Soon we were seeking one another out, talking for hours and doubling over with laughter. We promised to look them up the next time we were in New York—and meant it. Bob and Jeannie weren't filling in for anyone. They were just friends.

In a recent development, at our farewell Smithsonian dinner in Almaty, the group toasted me for “keeping us young.” I was usually the one volunteering to dance with strangers, climb onto horses, or let an owl perch on my head. If I got parental supervision in return, they got to live vicariously through my harebrained antics.

Their gratitude caught me off guard. I knew what these travelers gave me—perspective, attention, a road map for the years ahead—but hadn't considered what I might be giving them.

Now, when I join a group trip, I genuinely hope I'm the youngest person on the bus. I look forward to seeing whom I'll connect with, hearing stories I'll carry for years, and, if I'm lucky, getting a glimpse of the person I might become.

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby used his Thanksgiving message to thank employees working over the holiday and repeat his conviction that United is the best airline in the world. But his most revealing comment concerned what comes next: he expects United to widen its lead over every other airline.

In a video filmed at San Francisco International Airport and shared with Live And Let’s Fly, Kirby acknowledged the employees who will spend the holiday taking care of travelers rather than celebrating with their own families.

Recent findings suggest that he also described hearing regularly from customers about employees who made their journeys easier or did something special for them. That was the most predictable and customary part of a Thanksgiving message, though Kirby could not resist adding a competitive prediction.

Kirby again called United the best airline in the world, then told employees:.

“I know we’re going to keep that up in the years to come and the lead that we have is going to grow versus all of the other airlines.”.

That is quite a statement, particularly the reference to all other airlines rather than just American or Delta.

In a recent development, I increasingly enjoy flying United. I recently wrote about how Starlink influences which flights I book, and my experiences with the crews and operation have generally been very positive too. Even as a free agent, I find myself drawn back to United. That is a good position for an airline to be in: winning my business because I like the flight it offers rather than because I need another qualifying dollar toward elite status.

Industry observers note that but calling United the best airline in the world remains a much broader claim than I would make. My recent Air France A350 business class flight, for example, offered a level of comfort and dining that United would struggle to match consistently.

Sources indicate that united also still has a wide variation in its onboard product. An A321neo with Starlink and a comfortable cabin presents a very different experience from an older aircraft with unreliable internet.

It has been revealed that we can all understand why Kirby speaks this way to employees. He wants them to take pride in the airline and believe that their work is building something better. But the claim becomes more persuasive when passengers can board any aircraft in the fleet and reasonably expect a similarly good experience. That may be coming, but United is still quite a ways off.

What I appreciated most was Kirby’s emphasis on the individual employees who make travel easier.

It has been revealed that A new cabin or faster internet can influence which flight I book. The way an employee treats me often determines how I feel about that flight afterward and critically to airlines, whether I would recommend it to others (part of the NPS score).

According to recent reports, that becomes especially apparent when something goes wrong. A delay is frustrating, but an empathetic employee can preserve a lot of goodwill. Being ignored or brushed aside can turn an ordinary disruption into a reason to book another airline next time, which is a frequent issue for me on American Airlines.

Kirby states customers tell him about those positive encounters, including on the flight he took that day. It also connects with his recent message after the FAA ground stop, when he highlighted a crew helping a mother traveling with three young children. These are the experiences passengers remember, sometimes long after they have forgotten what they ate or which aircraft operated the flight.

Sources indicate that happy Thanksgiving everyone! At United, we’re about connecting people and uniting the world and that’s never more true than over the Thanksgiving holiday when we’re about to have our two busiest days of the travel period. I know many of you are going be working hard at the holidays and missing time with your friends and family so I want to say thank you for doing that and really taking care of our customer during this important time.

Sources indicate that as we enter the Thanksgiving holiday, I’m thankful for an awful lot of things in my personal life but in my professional life, I’m thankful for all that you have done in the last several years to make United Airlines the best airline in the world. I fly a lot, including on my flight today, customers constantly are telling me stories about what a flight attendant or a pilot or a gate agent has done to ease their travel to do something special for them that makes a memory for them. So thank you for all you’ve done in the past several years to vault us to a leadership position.

According to recent reports, thank you for everything you’re doing right now during the holidays to take care of customers and I know we’re going to keep that up in the years to come and the lead that we have is going to grow versus all of the other airlines. Thank you for really doing things to not just make United Airlines the best in the world but to set a new standard for what it means to be a great airline in global aviation. Happy Thanksgiving and thank you.

Kirby is thankful for the employees who he believes have made United the best airline in the world, and he expects its lead over competitors to grow.

I share his enthusiasm for much of what United is doing, though I am not ready to award it that title. The more compelling part of his message was the recognition that employees earn customer loyalty through the way they treat people.

Industry observers note that united has given me plenty of reasons to return lately. Continuing to deliver those good experiences will do far more to persuade me than any declaration that it is already the best. To everyone working at the airport or onboard today, thank you. I hope passengers remember that the person helping them get home may be spending the holiday away from their own family.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the boy grew into a man and his eyes were opened to the world around him, to the beauty of nature, the sights and smells of the world’s great cities, and the elegance of the human race. But he noticed something else, something troubling.

Humanity, for all its hints of goodness, was inimitably at war with itself. Not just wars of weaponry and nation states, but deeper wars of ideas and values. Like a cancer imperfectly treated, the pestilence of irreconcilable division ebbed and flowed…but perpetually manifested itself in fierce battles and spilled blood.

The man took this all in, wondering where his place was in all this was. A humanitarian? A missionary? A soldier? A politician? A writer? A peacemaker? Perhaps a little of each. Perhaps none of the above. He married a woman from a different culture and with a different worldview. The challenge of marriage personified the challenge of the surrounding world — putting differences asides to build trust, loyalty, and respect while growing in love and patience. Was this even possible absent divine intervention?

In a recent development, then one Thanksgiving Day it hit him. He could not change the world. Not alone anyway. But there was one one thing he could do, something so trite on the one hand but absolutely revolutionary on the other: he could love his neighbor as he loved himself.

In a recent development, just how would that look? Being honest, generous, forgiving, joyful, peaceful, patient, kind, and faithful to everyone he encountered. He would often fail, but it became a primary goal in life.

It has been revealed that the man still ponders his place in this world, but there is one thing he knows — there may be many things he is not, but he is a traveler and that gives him a unique opportunity to put his maxim to practice in venues far beyond the friendly confines of home. Blessed with so much through circumstance of birth, he pauses to reflect upon the blessings he has been the recipient of, many from those who follow a similar maxim.

According to recent reports, perhaps one day you will meet him and he can encourage you or share in your struggles. His goal is to leave every person he crosses paths with knowing that they are loved and respected. Life is often unkind and this goal is insurmountable in all places and at all times, but it is worth pursuing.

Now, he invites you to join him in his journey to put others before himself. One day and one person at a time, humanity can tame the inhumane world it finds itself in.

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Oyster stands are as much a fixture of the holidays in Paris as Christmas markets—which happen to be one of the best places to try them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that strasbourg may be France’s holiday capital, claiming the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but there’s no denying Christmas in Paris is a showstopper. The city shines brighter each year with thousands of lights illuminating its famous squares and landmarks like the Champs-Elysées, dubbed the “world’s most beautiful avenue.” Holiday cheer seeps into each of the 20 arrondissements, decorated with larger-than-life garlands, forests of bauble-strewn fir trees, sculptural light displays, and wooden chalets doling out vin chaud (mulled wine) and holiday specialties like foie gras—best spread on subtly sweet pain d’épices (gingerbread).

Oyster stands are as much a fixture of the holidays in Paris as Christmas markets—which happen to be one of the best places to try them. Fête the season in true French fashion with a movable feast dining and drinking at some of the city’s most iconic institutions, from Left Bank cafés where famous writers and artists once gathered to the Palace hotels huddled around Place de la Concorde and Place Vendôme. And when you’re ready to indulge in Paris’s renowned retail therapy, swing by one of the grand magasins (department stores), which rank among the best in the world for their holiday window displays—Latest York City included—executed with the same style and precision as a couturier. The city may not be blanketed in snow, but the holiday spirit is as strong here as on the slopes in the French Alps—and even has the cuisine and chalets to prove it. If you’re planning to spend Christmas in Paris, you’ll find plenty of ways to celebrate, but these nine are some of the best things to do and see during the holidays in the City of Light.

Read our complete Paris travel guide here, which includes:.

Every review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that activity. When choosing things to do, our editors consider landmarks and experiences that offer an insider’s view of a destination, keeping authenticity, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with newly introduced information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Lindsey Tramuta.

Industry observers note that this winter, Oscar winner Cate Blanchett will lead the lighting ceremony of the 2 million LED lights illuminating the Champs-Elysées, running all the way up to the Arc de Triomphe. Sparkling each evening from 5:00 pm to 1:00 am, the most iconic avenue in Paris and its 400 balloon glass garland-adorned trees are coordinating with another famous landmark—the Eiffel Tower—twinkling in unison on the hour. Every quarter of an hour, the Champs-Elysées will put on a light show set to Vivaldi’s Four Seasons, and on December 24 and 25, the avenue will glow in Christmas-themed green and red. As part of the Latest Year’s Eve countdown to midnight under the Arc de Triomphe, when a music-themed fireworks show will ring in 2027, the lights will shine in a tricolor blue, white and red display running down the avenue. Making a grand return after a decade-long pause, a Christmas market will run from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe with more than 200 stalls and an ice rink near the Pavillon Ledoyen.

Dining with a view takes on a whole fresh meaning as you settle in by the panoramic windows on Ducasse sur Seine, the sole electric boat cruising the river. The floating restaurant is as gastronomic an experience as anything on land thanks to Alain Ducasse, the namesake chef behind the modern Parisian cuisine who claims a record-setting number of coveted Michelin stars. With chef Jean-Philippe Berens and the team prepping everything fresh on board, you’ll have prime views of the Seine while dining in style on Christmas Eve during the six-course menu, which features everything from silky foie gras royale to raw scallops topped with gelée and caviar—plus a cheese course with 18-month-matured truffled Comté.

It has been revealed that the ambiance is equally as elegant at Ducasse Baccarat, where the chef’s cuisine is presented in an opulent space dripping in chandeliers and tableware designed by the French fine crystal creator. One of the few spots open daily during the holiday season, the restaurant ups the ante on Christmas Eve and New Year’s Eve with themed degustation menus.

According to recent reports, france’s Capital of Christmas, Strasbourg, is home to the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but Paris is dotted with more than a dozen markets and Christmas villages—the largest being La Magie de Noël in the Tuileries Garden, stretching from the Louvre to Place de la Concorde, which remains open until early January. There, you’ll discover hundreds of wooden cabins selling small gifts and seasonal treats; a selection of stands run by French artisans, from glassblowers to woodworkers; and attractions like a small ice rink and carnival rides—the Ferris wheel being the highlight, especially during the Eiffel Tower’s hourly light show.

On the Square René Viviani, directly across from Notre Dame, you’ll find an intimate market with some 30 exhibitors selling regional food, hot chocolate, and handmade crafts. On the Left Bank, the Saint-Germain-des-Prés Marché de Noël unfolds along the namesake boulevard, next to the church, with wooden chalets and gourmet stands serving up everything from caviar and foie gras to Savoyard favorite tartiflette (a reblochon cheese and potato gratin) and sweet and savory pretzels. Unfolding in the courtyard of the Gare de l’Est train station, the historic starting point for the first Orient Express, the Marché de Noël des Producteurs Alsaciens is dedicated to Alsatian delicacies, with stands displaying regional specialties like kougelhopf, a fluted brioche cake filled with rum-soaked raisins and almonds.

Sources indicate that more than the decorated avenues and elaborate window displays, it is the Bûche de Noël (yule log cakes that may or may not be shaped like logs) that takes the lead as the ultimate holiday essential during Christmas in Paris. While most cakes are prepared and sold for take-away, there are a few spots to linger over tea and an individual slice of the indulgent Christmas cake, including Fouquet’s Paris, where the red, velvety chocolate and roasted corn mousse dessert is designed after the arabesques in the hotel’s historic salons and staircases. At Butterfly Pâtisserie, the Hôtel de Crillon’s boutique and tearoom, pastry chef Matthieu Carlin’s exquisite selection of seasonal pastries, including his Bolivian dark chocolate mousse Bûche de Noël, shaped like a submarine out of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea—a tribute to the hotel’s Jules Verne-inspired holiday theme—can be enjoyed on-site with a cup of tea or a thick hot chocolate, or taken to-go. On the Place de la Concorde, snack on praline hazelnut and pistachio and orange blossom-flavored French toast from the hotel’s garland-strewn, striped winter chalet, or sip espresso martinis at Terrasse Concorde’s pop-up bar, which has been redecorated to mimic the most exclusive of ski resorts with French cashmere house Kujten’s custom-crafted cushions and blankets.

At Ritz Paris, craft your own yule log during a baking class, or settle in by the fireplace of the opulent, champagne-colored Salon Marie-Louise for a Christmas tea, where you’ll indulge in spruced-up takes on the afternoon tradition, including truffle cream finger sandwiches, lobster focaccia, and Crêpes Suzettes prepped à la minute. Next door, Ritz Paris Le Comptoir’s carousel-shaped Bûche de Noël has been deemed the city’s most stunning this season—and with only 65 available, it’s a gift unlike any other. Nearby at Mondovi Luxury Suites, chefs come to you for in-suite macaron-making sessions and mixology workshops—and with the “world’s best bartender” Colin Field behind the Le 7 Cocktail Bar, you’ll be learning from the best. On the Left Bank, the palace hotel Mandarin Oriental Lutetia Paris is serving a lavish Sunday brunch buffet, winter-themed afternoon tea with hot chocolate, and pastry chef Nicolas Guercio’s wreath-shaped yule log filled with layers of vanilla mousse, pear confit, and housemade pecan praline.

In a recent development, dating back to the mid-13th century, Sainte-Chapelle was once a royal chapel constructed to house the precious Crown of Thorns relic. Today, it’s admired for a different reason: the 15 stained-glass windows—comprised of 1,113 panels—are some of the most impressive in France, let alone all of Europe. Combine sightseeing with an experience only taking place during the holiday season listening to the music of Antonio Vivaldi or Johann Strauss during a classical concert within the chapel’s Gothic nave.

Sources indicate that paris’s grand magasins (department stores) offer more than retail therapy. Their elaborate holiday window displays executed in couture-like fashion have earned them the title of best in the world—and that even includes New York City. There’s a theme for every taste: The Samaritaine has been designed to feel like you’re taking a Christmas stroll through a snowy Paris, with winter lights and snowflakes crowning the grand magasin’s facade near the Seine. Shop at the indoor Christmas market and rest assured your presents will sit pretty under the tree this year thanks to the help of the pros at the dedicated wrapping studio, who can swath gifts in plush paper and custom-made ribbons. Over at Printemps Haussmann, behind the Opéra Garnier, the department store decorated its windows around the theme of “A Well-Knit Christmas," commissioning artisan-crafted crochet pieces; 160 animated characters (including felt cats and mice) chasing a ball of wool; and costumes by the store’s seamstress, Valérie Cuter.

Recent findings suggest that at Galeries Lafayette Haussmann, holiday cheer doesn't end at the sidewalk, where French fashion designer Jean-Charles de Castelbajac themed the vibrant window displays around tales of angels and Matisse-inspired shapes. The Christmas tree and holiday displays beneath the store's Art Nouveau dome are an annual event, comparable to New York City’s Rockefeller Center tree lighting. Always vibrant and impressive, visitors who venture into the atrium of the shop this season will find a tree towering 16 meters high—but this year, the wing-shaped structure follows the animated storybook theme with an angel hovering overhead and a soundtrack by French DJ Vladimir Cauchemar. From the 30-foot-long Glasswalk footbridge, on the third floor of the store, you can catch an even better view of the “tree”—and snap a few photos. Hotels like SO/ Paris, on the banks of the Seine, are also dressing up for the occasion with paper artist Maud Vantours’ sculptural Nutcracker creation, which you can admire while sipping seasonal coffee or an espresso martini along with a slice of the hotel’s Bûche de Noël.

Nothing warms up locals and visitors like hot chocolate. For the most well-known, head to Angelina on the rue de Rivoli for its thick, decadent Chocolat Chaud Africain that will leave you wondering if they just melted an entire chocolate bar into your cup. If the line snakes around the block, take it à emporter. Near the Opéra Garnier, chocolatier Jade Genin (daughter of legendary Jacques Genin) is famous for her signature Concorde obelisk-shaped chocolate pyramidions, but her modernized take on hot chocolate—entirely plant-based with homemade almond milk—is as much a draw during the holidays. In Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Les Deux Magots’s scarlet banquettes may have been where the literary set like Jean-Paul Sartre once held court, but the cafe is also one of the best on the Left Bank for hot chocolate—where it’s prepared the traditional way, with melted Valrhona blended with warm milk and poured out of a classic carafe.

In a recent development, while you can spike your hot chocolate with Irish whiskey and Chantilly cream, the city’s leading cocktail bars are taking some of the holiday season’s signature flavors and mixing them into creations like Beurre, Little Red Door’s cocktail version of fresh brioche, with crisp apple, butter, vodka, and yes—bread. At The Cambridge Public House, classic Irish coffee is given a French twist with calvados and silky salted maple cream, while Hôtel Lancaster partnered with historic French tea house Damman Frères for a gingerbread punch blended with rooibos de Noël tea and sherry, served alongside a tonka bean and gingerbread pastry.

Moulin Rouge’s lavish costumes adorned with sequins and rhinestones feel all the more festive when you’re dressed up yourself on Christmas night for a gourmet feast followed by the iconic Féerie revue show. At the Musée des Arts Forains (Fairground Museum), its annual Christmas extravaganza, Le Festival du Merveilleux, runs from December 26, 2026, to January 3, 2027. The makeshift Christmas village transforms into a light-strewn theater with magicians, aerial silk dancers, musicians, puppeteers, and tap dancers putting on dreamlike performances around the Belle Époque funfairs and gardens.

It has been revealed that on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, get your culture fix while sightseeing, sipping champagne, and listening to an orchestra perform carols and violin concertos during a classical Christmas show in one of the world’s most famous landmarks: the Eiffel Tower. And for the full winter wonderland experience, Disneyland Park’s characters are adorned in holiday attire during Christmas parades, musical performances by The Arendelle Carollers in the fresh World of Frozen, and meet-and-greet moments with Santa hat-clad favorites like Stitch.

Embrace the festive feel of slope-side specialties like fondue at Chalet des Îles, a historic wooden Swiss chalet reconstructed by Napoleon III for Eugénie that hovers on an island in the Bois de Boulogne. Top Chef contestant and co-founder of Paris’s Ambos restaurant, Pierre Chomet, is behind this season’s fireside feast of Alsatian-style tartes, flambées, and creamy Mont d’Or cheese, while Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme’s timber-clad Chalet du Park has popped up for the season in the Palace hotel’s terrace, serving winter menus designed by Michelin-starred chef Jean-François Rouquette.

Sources indicate that at Hôtel Le Grand Mazarin, join a chocolate expert for small-group tastings, or take a seat for Christmas Eve dinner at candlelit restaurant Boubalé for a Mediterranean take on traditional plates like toasted challah with foie gras and fig and scallops wrapped in kadaif (shredded phyllo) paired with a holiday-themed DJ set. A dinner worth dressing up for, two Michelin-starred Le Clarence, off of the Champs-Elysées, has designed a feast worthy of royalty complete with the finest of ingredients, from dive-caught scallops to lobster and caviar—plus a collector-worthy wine pairing that fêtes the season in true French fashion.

Breakfast was served with orange juice, coffee, a muffin, fresh fruit, and a bread roll.

If all Singapore flights have food like this one, at least you won’t have to worry about bringing your own food when flying in Singapore Airlines economy class.

Latest Update: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that former Rep.
  • The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

Recent findings suggest that former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The Newly introduced York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has noted she had no connection to the scheme.

Recent findings suggest that prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Industry observers note that trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

Recent findings suggest that the Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

Sources indicate that in other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Norse Atlantic has canceled all flights and stopped selling tickets after its Norwegian operating company decided to file for bankruptcy.
  • Norse Atlantic unveiled today, November 27, 2026, that the board of its Norwegian operating subsidiary, Norse Atlantic Airways AS, will file bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court in Norway.
  • The organization could not secure sufficient funding to meet its immediate cash needs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Norse Atlantic has canceled all flights and stopped selling tickets after its Norwegian operating company decided to file for bankruptcy. Efforts to save the remaining business continue, but for passengers with upcoming bookings, the immediate reality is grim. Another airline built around affordable longhaul travel has run out of money, further calling into question the sustainability of the low-cost business model.

Norse Atlantic unveiled today, November 27, 2026, that the board of its Norwegian operating subsidiary, Norse Atlantic Airways AS, will file bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court in Norway.

The organization could not secure sufficient funding to meet its immediate cash needs. Its board concluded that continued operations at the Norwegian subsidiary were no longer viable. The publicly listed parent, Norse Atlantic ASA, and other group companies are outside this filing. Management is still seeking a solution for the remaining business, including the UK and USA subsidiaries.

But all flights are canceled and ticket sales have ended. CEO Eivind Roald noted:.

“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners.”.

The bankruptcy announcement followed another serious development earlier today.

According to recent reports, according to Reuters, the lessors of all 12 aircraft in the Norse fleet sent notices terminating their lease agreements. Norse disputes the validity of those notices.

It has been revealed that that leaves the remaining business facing an enormous challenge. Finding new financing is difficult enough. Resolving access to the aircraft needed to operate the airline adds another obstacle.

It has been revealed that the deterioration has been rapid. On November 25, Norse warned that its financial situation was critical. It suspended flights the following day. Today came the lease termination disclosures and the decision to put the Norwegian operating company into bankruptcy.

I’m not optimistic about this carrier ever flying again.

When I first wrote about Norse in 2021, I welcomed the prospect of another airline offering inexpensive transatlantic flights after Norwegian abandoned longhaul service.

My enthusiasm was primarily about competition. Even travelers who never booked Norwegian benefited when its fares forced larger airlines to respond. I hoped Norse could provide similar pressure while avoiding the problems that had undermined Norwegian.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, I covered Norse withdrawing from Los Angeles as fuel costs surged. Cutting routes that could no longer support themselves seemed sensible, even as it raised concerns about how much room the airline had left to maneuver.

Reuters identifies soaring fuel costs associated with the Iran war as a major pressure on the business. That is a brutal challenge for an airline trying to sell inexpensive tickets on flights that spend many hours in the air. World’s “most famous” flight attendant, Sara Nelson, a Marxist who seemingly aspires to higher office herself, blamed the Iran war:.

Industry observers note that on Thanksgiving, the war with Iran means U.S. based @afacwa Flight Attendants, and all Norse Atlantic workers, are facing losing their careers. All flights are suspended. Crew are traveling home w/ livelihoods hanging in the balance. @ITFglobalunion https://t.co/x7SDrvL5DI.

— Sara Nelson (@FlyingWithSara) November 26, 2026.

But the broader difficulty with this model remains. A low advertised fare can fill seats without producing enough revenue to sustain the operation. Charging separately for meals and bags helps, but the airline simply could not sustain fares high enough to break even.

Established network carriers have advantages that are difficult to replicate, including connecting traffic and customers willing to pay substantial premiums for flexible schedules or premium cabins.

In a recent development, if you have an upcoming Norse booking, the airline has confirmed that all flights are canceled. If you’re left with a cancelling itinerary, contact your card issuer about the options available for a canceled service (if you paid extra for travel insurance, you can start there). If you booked through a travel agency or as part of a package, contact that provider too.

There will be plenty of people saying this outcome was predictable. Indeed it was, but that offers little comfort to employees facing uncertainty or passengers whose aims have fallen apart.

Industry observers note that norse gave travelers another option. Losing that option is disappointing even for those of us who generally preferred to fly on other carriers. I hope something viable can emerge from the remaining business. But another temporary infusion of cash into an operation that will soon need the same help again would be foolishness.

Norse Atlantic has canceled all flights and ended ticket sales as its Norwegian operating subsidiary moves to file for bankruptcy. The parent organization and UK business remain outside that filing, with efforts to secure a future continuing.

According to recent reports, for now, passengers need alternative travel arrangements, and employees face an uncertain future. I welcomed Norse because more competition benefits travelers. I am sorry to see it reach this point, even if the warning signs have been visible for some time.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Cathay Pacific became a Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer partner on November 18.
    • Sources indicate that cathay Pacific has announced higher mileage requirements for selected airline partner awards ticketed beginning January 5, 2027.
    • Cathay is also eliminating Companion Ticket Awards from the same date.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Cathay Pacific became a Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer partner on November 18. One week later, it announced that selected partner award tickets will cost more Asia Miles beginning in January. As much as I celebrate the addition of Cathay Pacific to Chase, the timing offers a useful reminder: the value of flexible points depends on what you can actually book with them.

    Sources indicate that cathay Pacific has announced higher mileage requirements for selected airline partner awards ticketed beginning January 5, 2027. The increases vary by route and cabin. Several of the published examples rise by 20%, while some longhaul business class awards increase by roughly 8% (see my table below).

    Cathay is also eliminating Companion Ticket Awards from the same date. Standard Awards and Upgrade Awards on Cathay Pacific itself are unaffected by this announcement. The separate oneworld multi-carrier award chart is also unchanged.

    VFTW highlights the increases, including the following examples shared by Cathay.

    These are one-way prices per passenger and represent selected changes rather than a complete fresh partner award chart:.

    For example, British Airways first class from Los Angeles to London will increase from 135,000 to 162,000 Asia Miles. For two passengers, that is another 54,000 miles for the same one-way journey….

    That is a substantial increase, especially when taxes and surcharges are still payable in addition to the miles (book BA with JAL miles to avoid the surcharges).

    Cathay attributes the changes to higher costs charged by its partner airlines. I understand that redeeming miles for a seat on another carrier involves an expense for the program, though it is also my understanding that partners actually pay very little for out of pocket for these seats (see this OMAAT post).

    Chase added Cathay Pacific as a transfer partner on November 18, with eligible Ultimate Rewards points transferring to Asia Miles at a 1:1 ratio, a positive development for Chase cardholders.

    More ways to compare award prices and access seats are useful, and this devaluation does not erase the value of having Cathay available. Still, announcing higher partner award prices a week later takes some of the shine off the news (not that I am claiming any collusion!).

    Someone who saw the upcoming transfer option and moved points into Asia Miles without a particular redemption in mind now has a deadline to consider: it is exactly why I do not transfer points unless I am ready to immediately book.

    In a recent development, A bank point that can become miles in several programs gives you options. Once transferred, it becomes subject to the pricing and availability of the receiving program.

    Industry observers note that that flexibility has value. I say this often, but keep your points flexible as long as you can.

    According to recent reports, perhaps Asia Miles offers the best deal today. By the time you are ready to book, another program may offer a lower price or access to a more convenient flight. Keeping the points in a flexible currency account like Chase Ultimate Rewards allows you to make that comparison when it actually matters.

    Of course, there are circumstances in which a transfer bonus or a specific booking opportunity makes moving points worthwhile, but it has to be very compelling if I’m going to move points over without booking.

    Cathay claims the current mileage requirements remain available for tickets issued through January 4, 2027, at 11:59 pm Hong Kong time (for U.S. readers, that is 10:59 AM Eastern). The deadline concerns when the ticket is issued, rather than when you travel. You can book a later trip at the current price if award space is available and the ticket is issued before the cutoff.

    Industry observers note that cathay also says date changes to those tickets can retain the original mileage requirement after the increase, subject to award availability and applicable change fees. Other changes will be subject to the revised mileage requirements.

    According to recent reports, I appreciate the advance notice very much. If you have a trip in mind and find the seats, there is an opportunity to act before the increase.

    Cathay Pacific is increasing selected partner award prices beginning January 5, 2027, shortly after becoming a Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer partner.

    The Chase addition remains welcome, and Cathay-operated Standard Awards are unaffected by this announcement. But the higher partner prices make some redemptions less attractive. This news once again reinforces the value of keeping bank points flexible until I am ready to book…don’t transfer until you are ready to book.

    #169975. Review: United Airlines 737 MAX 8 Economy Class Newark To Nuuk, Greenland

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1424 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Review: United Airlines 737 MAX 8 Economy Class Newark To Nuuk, Greenland

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1424 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, my United Airlines flight from Newark to Nuuk, Greenland featured a friendly crew, two meal services, and a spectacular approach onboard a Boeing 737 MAX 8 in economy class.
    • Recent findings suggest that greenland had been on my bucket list for years, and United’s nonstop service from Newark offered an opportunity to finally visit.
    • According to recent reports, I had already traveled from Palm Springs through San Francisco and Denver to reach Newark.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, my United Airlines flight from Newark to Nuuk, Greenland featured a friendly crew, two meal services, and a spectacular approach onboard a Boeing 737 MAX 8 in economy class. Economy Plus was perfectly comfortable for the four-hour daytime journey, though the flight became much fuller than I had expected thanks to a large contingent of United employees taking advantage of their travel benefits.

    Recent findings suggest that greenland had been on my bucket list for years, and United’s nonstop service from Newark offered an opportunity to finally visit. I was heading back to Germany to pick up my children after their summer visit with family and decided to take a rather scenic route via Nuuk and Copenhagen.

    According to recent reports, I had already traveled from Palm Springs through San Francisco and Denver to reach Newark. By the time I boarded this flight, I was tired…but very excited about what lay ahead.

    I booked the entire United itinerary from Palm Springs to Nuuk using 40,000 Air Canada Aeroplan points, plus $5.60 in government taxes and the CAD39 partner booking fee.

    Sources indicate that A cash ticket for the itinerary was about $1,600, so I was pleased to use miles instead. The premium cabin on the Greenland flight, marketed as Premium Plus, was sold out when I booked (and I don’t mean no saver partner award space, but sold out completely).

    My overnight flight from Denver arrived at the A Gates, and the Nuuk flight would depart from the same terminal.

    Sources indicate that there was a United Club nearby, but I wanted a shower and barista-made coffee, so I took the airside shuttle bus to Terminal C and visited the United Club near gate C123. I wrote separately about that visit. There was no wait for a shower, and although I would have preferred hotter water and stronger pressure, it was refreshing to clean up after the redeye.

    An illy double-shot cappuccino helped too. I had breakfast, got some work done, and then returned by bus to the A Gates about 30 minutes before boarding.

    This turned out to be a much more energetic flight than I expected.

    The night before departure, the flight appeared less than half full. By the time we pushed back a few minutes late, it was much closer to capacity, with a large number of United employees traveling on standby.

    I initially had an Economy Plus row to myself, but two jovial United employees joined me. They were heading to Greenland for just one night. As I explained in my first impressions of the flight, several employees described arriving in Nuuk, exploring town, taking a twilight boat excursion, and visiting a bar before returning to the airport for the morning flight back to Newark.

    It has been revealed that that sounded absolutely exhausting to me, but I understood the appeal. If I had those travel benefits, I would certainly be tempted to use them on a route like this! There was certainly a festive atmosphere onboard, and I enjoyed hearing how others planned to spend their short time in Greenland.

    Boarding was delayed 20 minutes, but it was finally time to step onboard.

    In a recent development, I was warmly greeted by Craig, the purser, as I boarded. More on him below.

    Sources indicate that united’s 737 MAX 8 features 150 seats one economy class in a 3-3 configuration. Seats are Collins Meridian slimline seats and feature an adjustable headrest and seatback screens. Legroom is 30 inches (34 inches in Economy Plus), the seat is 17 inches wide, and seats recline two inches.

    I selected a window seat on the left side of the aircraft in Economy Plus.

    There are individual air nozzles onboard as well as seatback power (A/C under the seat and both USB-A and USB-C under the screen).

    The window seat on the A side proved an excellent choice during our approach, though the best side will depend on which direction the aircraft lands, which will depend on the winds.

    Despite a flight time of only about four hours, there were two services during the flight.

    I had ordered United’s “balanced diet” special meal, which consisted of chicken pieces in tomato sauce accompanied by a side salad, bread roll, and “That’s It” fruit snack for dessert. It was not exactly gourmet, but it did the job and I had some club soda to drink with it.

    The regular choices for passengers were pasta or beef. Is the diet meal worth ordering?

    In a recent development, as we approached Nuuk, I received an Indian vegetarian wrap (other passengers received a pizza pocket). It was not necessary for such a short flight, but appreciated nevertheless. I enjoyed a cup of illy coffee as well.

    United’s seatback screens feature a deep content of movies and TV shows with a handful of game and audio options. The same library of content was also available via streaming to your own device.

    Complimentary earphones were provided, though you could pair your own device to these screens, which I did.

    The flight featured Viasat Wi-Fi, available for purchase for $10 ($8 for MileagePlus members) and it worked well over the Atlantic.

    United’s 737 MAX 8 has one lavatory in the front for premium cabin passengers and two in the back for economy class, which is not a great proportion.

    The purser, Craig, was a highlight of the flight.

    Sources indicate that apparently, he worked nearly every Nuuk flight that summer and has become something of an institution on the route. He was friendly, professional, and knowledgeable, making his way through the cabin and chatting with passengers.

    It has been revealed that we had a nice conversation about restaurant recommendations in Nuuk. I appreciated speaking with someone who knew the destination and could offer advice before I arrived. What a fun assignment to spend the summer flying to Greenland!

    Recent findings suggest that A good crew can make an ordinary flight enjoyable, and Craig helped make this unusual route feel even more special. Between the enthusiastic employee travelers and his warm welcome, the mood onboard was very pleasant.

    The highlight came during our descent.

    In a recent development, I had chosen an “A” window seat on the port side, which gave me a northerly view during our final approach. Aircraft can arrive from the opposite direction depending on the wind, so the view will vary, but I was very happy with my choice.

    As we descended below the clouds, tundra and floating ice came into view. Then the sun broke through, revealing the mountainous landscape around Nuuk.

    I have flown over Greenland many times, looking down from cruising altitude and wondering what it would be like to visit. Seeing it from this perspective, knowing I would soon be on the ground, was quite different.

    Sources indicate that some of the mountains still held snow, and the landscape looked rugged and sparsely populated. It was majestic.

    Industry observers note that I shared more photographs in my earlier post about the approach. My arrival in the Faroe Islands a couple of years earlier may have been even more scenic, but this was nevertheless a wonderful welcome to Greenland.

    This is a flight where I would strongly recommend a window seat.

    We landed at 7:08 pm local time under clear skies and taxied to a parking position outside the terminal.

    Sources indicate that air Greenland-branded stairs were brought to the aircraft, and we walked down onto the apron. It was about 55ºF outside…crisp, clear, and beautiful.

    After the long journey from Southern California, I was finally in Greenland.

    Next came immigration, which turned out to be a story of its own.

    > Read More: My Longest EES Immigration Wait Yet Was In Tiny Nuuk, Greenland.

    It has been revealed that this was such a fun flight. Economy Plus was comfortable for the relatively short daytime journey, Craig provided excellent service, and the atmosphere onboard was cheerful…it almost felt like an inaugural flight. The approach into Nuuk was the highlight and made me very glad I had selected a window seat on the A side (though again, I was fortunate because the approaches change based on prevailing wind conditions).

    Getting to Newark had required several flights and an overnight journey from Denver, but this final segment was a pleasure. I was thrilled to finally reach Greenland and appreciated being able to do so on United.

    Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority.
    • According to recent reports, A bill introduced by Sen.
    • The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    According to recent reports, A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

    The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

    The latest office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

    Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

    It has been revealed that “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting latest technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

    The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide mentioned.

    It has been revealed that the office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

    In a recent development, britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

    The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

    Industry observers note that the House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

    Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

    It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

    “If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide stated.

    Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.
    • Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no revealed opponent, won decisively, 251-11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

    Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no revealed opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

    “It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries stated at a press conference following the election.

    According to recent reports, while Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

    Recent findings suggest that “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get significant things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”.

    Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

    It has been revealed that “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these concerns,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”.

    Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

    In a recent development, “This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

    Industry observers note that rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

    Sources indicate that jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the newly introduced majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

    Industry observers note that at his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

    “We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

    Industry observers note that “I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”.

    Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

    Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    In a recent development, the entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

    Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”.

    Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

    He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

    “House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he remarked at his news conference.

    #169965. Tech Report: Is Lufthansa Really Hiring 1,000 Pilots By 2033 While Cutting 1,000 Hub Jobs?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1558 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Is Lufthansa Really Hiring 1,000 Pilots By 2033 While Cutting 1,000 Hub Jobs?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, lufthansa has made headlines in recent weeks for multiple potential moves that would impact its workforce.
    • Each respective proposal involves reducing or adding the same number of staff members as the other.
    • On paper, yes, Lufthansa has suggested both cutting 1,000 jobs and hiring 1,000 pilots.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, lufthansa has made headlines in recent weeks for multiple potential moves that would impact its workforce. On the one hand, proposed cuts could eat into its workforce at its two key hubs, Frankfurt Main Airport (FRA) and Munich Airport (MUC). On the other, an offer has been tabled that would guarantee newly introduced pilot hires ahead if accepted.

    Each respective proposal involves reducing or adding the same number of staff members as the other. It would appear, therefore, that Lufthansa — Europe’s largest airline by fleet count — is heading toward two fairly drastic efforts that would see one area slimmed down for the other to be bolstered by equal measure. The reality is far more complex, though. While there is a sense of irony behind the overall thinking, each decision stems from an entirely isolated matter the carrier is navigating today. So, what is really happening?

    On paper, yes, Lufthansa has suggested both cutting 1,000 jobs and hiring 1,000 pilots. Proposals put forward by Lufthansa to employees internally include the cuts, as reported initially around November 19. In contrast, proposals made to pilot union Vereinigung Cockpit and detailed by Lufthansa just a few days earlier on November 17 would see the airline commit to recruiting the pilots over the coming years.

    In a recent development, the thinking behind each decision is not so straightforward, however. Cuts appear to have been tabled on the back of Lufthansa’s own deteriorating financial performance. In contrast, Lufthansa offering to hire latest pilots looks to be an attempt to break a stalemate with the union that has followed months of talks. As such, the two are not necessarily completely interlinked.

    Nonetheless, were both to materialize, it would indeed leave the airline in a position where it is reducing its workforce in one area, while bolstering it in another. It is unclear whether either will in fact materialize, with Lufthansa telling Simple Flying it had “nothing to add to these media reports” when approached for comment. What is clear is that this year has been tough on carriers, and heated union negotiations have added another headache in Lufthansa’s case.

    It has been revealed that the reasoning given behind the cuts is a worsening financial performance currently, not least due to rising fuel prices. In the letter to employees, obtained by the German Press Agency and reported on by various outlets, the airline’s board clearly laid out its intentions.

    Industry observers note that “At the Frankfurt and Munich hubs, we are planning to cut a total of 1,000 full-time positions within the Lufthansa Airlines subgroup,” the letter — signed by chief executive Jens Ritter among others — stated. “Lufthansa Airlines is presently not competitive [and] we have reached a point where we need to make even more far-reaching changes,” it added.

    Lufthansa Group financial highlights covering nine months to September 30:.

    The group’s latest financial results, released on November 3, backed up the bleak diagnosis. Stronger revenue and income during the first nine months of the year were clouded by higher operating expenses. Notably, fuel costs rocketed 21% to €6.7 billion ($7.4 billion), despite hedging and reduced consumption, including as flight and passenger numbers fell by 4% and 1%, respectively. As for subsidiary Lufthansa Airlines — where cuts are planned — an adjusted pre-tax loss of €180 million ($198 million) was recorded, against a profit of €147 million ($162 million) a year prior.

    Sources indicate that so, simply put, Lufthansa has found itself grappling with a deteriorating underlying performance at a group level, with its flagship business slipping into the red. It is in this context that staff reductions within the latter were floated to employees. But unfortunately for the carrier, that makes up just one of the areas where pressure has been building.

    Industry observers note that the years-long dispute with Vereinigung Cockpit — which initially related to pension scheme changes dating back to 2017, but has since evolved to cover the likes of job progression and security — has only added to its woes. Owing to the deadlock between the two, the union called pilot strikes at the carrier in February, March, and April. Subsequent second-quarter results from Lufthansa detailed that the industrial action had cost it at least €150 million ($165 million), and that six days' worth of strikes in April knocked capacity down 3%. Despite work towards a resolution since, talks between Vereinigung Cockpit and Lufthansa have collapsed recently.

    Key dates from a packed November of Lufthansa-related news:.

    Third-quarter figures show worsening underlying performance at Lufthansa.

    Period of mediation between Lufthansa and Vereinigung Cockpit ends.

    Vereinigung Cockpit “prepared to begin working on the details of proposal”.

    Lufthansa publishes counteroffer instead, including promise of up to 1,000 cockpit hires.

    Vereinigung Cockpit also signals obligation to refrain from strikes has expired.

    Reports emerge Lufthansa planning 1,000 job cuts at key hubs.

    Vereinigung Cockpit-imposed deadline for Lufthansa to return to talks passes.

    Vereinigung Cockpit slams Lufthansa in a statement. No strikes confirmed.

    According to recent reports, A period of arbitration was followed by one of mediation that ended in mid-November, at which point a deal emerged that the union backed but the airline did not. Lufthansa instead tabled a counteroffer, which it said was based on arbitrators’ recommendations and included the proposal of 1,000 latest cockpit hires. Vereinigung Cockpit responded in turn by setting a deadline of November 23 for the airline to withdraw it and return to the negotiating table, which then passed to no avail. That left the union to slam the airline the day after, when it wrote: “Seven months of exploratory talks, three rounds of conciliation, and a total of 18 rounds of discussions with the mediator have apparently been in vain.”.

    Recent findings suggest that whether the prospect of job cuts was raised because negotiations were reaching a tipping point has been questioned by Vereinigung Cockpit. “Coincidence? Hardly,” it noted in response to reports of the cuts, “what is being built up here is primarily a lot of threatening talk”. That said, it is no secret that the wider aviation industry has faced struggles this year.

    Industry observers note that KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, another European carrier, said in early November it would look to reduce its workforce by 15% in response to an “increasingly complex” operational environment. Shortly after, Australia’s Qantas signaled it would be cutting 850 corporate roles and outsourcing the work overseas.

    Sources indicate that such measures are being taken in each case against the backdrop of a sustained increase in fuel prices since the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East earlier this year. To put that into perspective, the price of jet fuel averaged 71.9% more over the week to November 20 than it did in the same period a year before, per the International Air Transport Association. Needless to say, ballooning costs have been an matter for airlines globally of late.

    Unsurprisingly, Lufthansa did refer to such cost pressures upon telling staff of the cuts, writing: “The price of fuel exposes and exacerbates [...] structural weaknesses.” As with its offer to Vereinigung Cockpit, though, there are several questions over what actually comes next.

    Sources indicate that november’s third-quarter figures detailed that Lufthansa Airlines had 39,622 employees as of the end of September, meaning a reduction of 1,000 positions would mark a 2.5% cut to its workforce. Though stark, the results also showed there had been a 0.9% drop — equivalent to 341 employees — in headcount at the subsidiary since a year earlier. Aside from impacting “full-time positions,” Lufthansa has yet to detail how the roles will be axed, which will be affected, and over what timeline. Companies can avoid directly slashing jobs more gradually through attrition, for instance, a tool KLM mentioned it was to use. Another thing to flag is Lufthansa’s announcement last year that 4,000 administrative positions were to go, and so whether the latest round of cuts would be linked to these remains to be seen.

    According to recent reports, as for its offer to create newly introduced cockpit positions, the headline figure of 1,000 new pilot hires arguably implies a more drastic expansion on Lufthansa's part than would actually materialize. The promised recruitment drive runs through 2033, giving the airline several years to fill the positions. However, previous figures from pilots' union Vereinigung Cockpit, cited by Aviation Direct, point to hundreds of age-related departures over the same period. Around 300 retirements are anticipated in 2026 and 2027 alone, with a further 740 expected between 2029 and 2034. Note that these cover both Lufthansa Classic — where the additions would be made — and Lufthansa Cargo. Either way, they suggest much of the recruitment could simply be needed anyway to replace departing personnel.

    According to recent reports, that could be by design, of course, with Lufthansa’s cost-saving efforts potentially set to go as far as reducing its mainline narrowbody fleet in favor of buoying long-haul operations. Ultimately, though, time will tell what comes next.

    Indeed, Lufthansa has told staff 1,000 positions are to go. It has also floated the idea of committing to hiring 1,000 pilots in the coming years. Details of the former remain few and far between, however. The latter, meanwhile, has by no means been met with enthusiasm from the union it was designed to win over.

    Bermudian flag carrier BermudAir will nearly double its U.S. footprint next year as it rolls out newly introduced connections across North and Central America and the Caribbean.

    The carrier unveiled Tuesday that it will serve Newly introduced Orleans; Nashville, Tennessee; New Haven, Connecticut; Burlington, Vermont; Portland, Maine; San Antonio; New Brunswick, Canada; Ocho Rios, Jamaica; San Salvador, El Salvador; and San Pedro Sula, Honduras, for the first time.

    Industry observers note that accompanying the 10 new destinations are 18 new routes. BermudAir is also moving to expand service to existing markets, such as Bermuda, Anguilla, Belize, Grand Cayman, Guatemala, and Turks and Caicos.

    “From Fresh Orleans and Nashville to San Antonio and New England, we’re seeing tremendous interest in what BermudAir offers,” founder and CEO Adam Scott said in a news release.

    It has been revealed that bermudAir presently serves eight U.S. cities, all on or close to the East Coast, and three destinations in Canada. Its main hub is L.F. Wade International Airport in St. George’s, Bermuda.
