    Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of problems even as he appears politically weakened at home.

    Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

    It has been revealed that the U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

    Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, remarked Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one problem with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

    According to recent reports, “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

    It has been revealed that still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”.

    Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

    “They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

    That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

    “I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump mentioned Monday. “I think he's backing down.”.

    Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a significant reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

    In a recent development, senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, remarked Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”.

    “I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”.

    Recent findings suggest that during remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

    “Enforcement of the latest rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat stated, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

    Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

    “Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”.

    But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

    Sources indicate that he stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

    Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”.

    Sources indicate that trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the firm’s president and CEO. He also mentioned he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

    Sources indicate that the administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”.

    Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Challenges at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”.

    It has been revealed that “Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”.

    • Industry observers note that norse flew just one U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Norse Atlantic Airways is no more.

    The Norway-based long-haul budget airline officially ceased operations and filed for bankruptcy on Friday after failing to raise the cash necessary to keep flying.

    The bankruptcy filing comes two days after Pakistan International Airlines, which contracts Norse to operate select flights, mentioned on X that Norse had suspended operations "without prior notice.".

    Industry observers note that norse flew just one U.S. route at the time of its shut down: Orlando International Airport (MCO) to London's Gatwick Airport (LGW), schedules from aviation analytics firm Cirium show.

    Sources indicate that during the prime summer months, Norse also seasonally flew from Upcoming York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Athens International Airport (ATH) in Greece, LGW and Rome's Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO).

    At its peak in 2024, Norse served five U.S. destinations, including Las Vegas's Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), from gateways in Europe.

    It has been revealed that the collapse of Norse comes at a challenging time for airlines. Jet fuel is at historic highs, spiking after Iran war and other conflicts. Geopolitical tensions have closed significant swaths of airspace, including Russia and significant portions of the Middle East. And, high interest rates have pushed the cost of capital for any business to the highest levels in years.

    Norse warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical" and said its continued operation was "dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs.".

    Luis Gallego, the CEO of International Airlines Group that owns British Airways and Iberia, told the Financial Times in October that smaller airlines would struggle this winter due to the those financial headwinds.

    Norse was one of the last airlines trying to make long-haul, low-cost work between the U.S. and Europe. Play Airlines, which attempted the same strategy via a connecting hub at Iceland's Keflavik International Airport (KEF), shut down in September 2025. And both Norse and Play were formed following the retrenchment and collapse of previous attempts; Norse from Norwegian Air's withdrawal from the market in 2021 and Play from the ashes of WOW Air that shut down in 2019.

    Only independent French Bee and the budget arms of the larger European airline groups, including Discover, Level and Edelweiss Air, continue to offer lower-cost transatlantic flights.

    Story updated with Norse confirmation of its shut down and subsequent bankruptcy filing.

    #169956. Breaking: FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (893 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.
    • Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    Recent findings suggest that thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz mentioned at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    Sources indicate that “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they noted.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about intends for such an inquiry.

    Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter mentioned.

    On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related concerns,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján stated, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    In a recent development, sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., mentioned at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    It has been revealed that “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that glitch,” Moran noted.

    Moran also mentioned he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

    FAA Projects Busiest Thanksgiving Travel Week in 16 Years

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, more than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S.
    • If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.
    • Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, more than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S. this week and early next week as Americans travel ahead of and after Thanksgiving, according to the FAA.

    If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.

    Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.

    Sources indicate that air traffic will dip only slightly on Wednesday (49,831 flights) and nearly halve on Thanksgiving Day (27,619 flights) itself, the FAA noted, with a rebound following Friday to Tuesday, Dec. 1. There will be over 50,000 flights per day on the Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday after Thanksgiving.

    Perhaps aiming to assuage concerns from the public after a turbulent couple of weeks, transportation officials said they are prioritizing traveler safety and taking “unprecedented action” to limit flight delays and cancellations.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that the Trump administration has assembled a “tiger team” of experts to prevent another mass ground stop.

    According to recent reports, “Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford mentioned in a statement. “The growing demand for air travel makes it more crucial than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century.”.

    In a recent development, the FAA is also advising travelers to get to the airport early and check with their airline for updates if bad weather seems likely to impact their trip. The agency noted the high likelihood of thunderstorms in the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast this week.

    #169953. Why Cargolux Won Approval To Fly Boeing 747 Freighters To An Airport Most Flyers Have Never Heard Of

    Why Cargolux Won Approval To Fly Boeing 747 Freighters To An Airport Most Flyers Have Never Heard Of

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, on November 17, 2026, Uzbekistan's civil aviation authority granted Luxembourg-based Cargolux Airlines a permit to operate scheduled cargo flights to Navoi International Airport (NVI) with Boeing 747F freighters.
    • For most travelers, Navoi barely registers on the aviation map, but freight planners are looking closely at what the airport offers.
    • Sources indicate that uzbekistan's civil aviation regulator, the Uzaviation Agency, granted Cargolux Airlines a permit to operate scheduled Boeing 747F cargo services to Navoi International Airport, setting the scene for one of the more intriguing route expansions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, on November 17, 2026, Uzbekistan's civil aviation authority granted Luxembourg-based Cargolux Airlines a permit to operate scheduled cargo flights to Navoi International Airport (NVI) with Boeing 747F freighters. The surprise is that a major widebody cargo carrier, operating a 30-aircraft fleet of Boeing 747-400Fs and 747-8Fs, is betting on Navoi as a pure-play cargo hub with a free customs zone as opposed to focusing on Tashkent, the Uzbek capital.

    For most travelers, Navoi barely registers on the aviation map, but freight planners are looking closely at what the airport offers. Why would one of the world's largest cargo airlines pursue regulatory approval for a small Central Asian airport before announcing a launch date, frequency, routing, payload, or European network link? For Cargolux, opting for an airport out of the spotlight may just be one of the best moves available.

    Sources indicate that uzbekistan's civil aviation regulator, the Uzaviation Agency, granted Cargolux Airlines a permit to operate scheduled Boeing 747F cargo services to Navoi International Airport, setting the scene for one of the more intriguing route expansions. The authorization builds on earlier bilateral aviation ties, including a 2019 air traffic protocol designed to support Cargolux transit cargo flows to Asian markets starting in 2020.

    Recent findings suggest that an important shift in how Navoi is governed helps explain why the hub is drawing direct freighter interest now. Navoi International Airport was decoupled from centralized operational control under Uzbekistan Airports LLC in 2026, gaining commercial autonomy to negotiate agreements directly with international airlines and logistics partners, as reported by the Tashkent Times.

    Operating independently lets Navoi tailor slot coordination, ground arrangements, and commercial terms to cargo operators rather than competing for attention inside a passenger-led airport group. Navoi reinforced that cargo-first positioning in October 2026 with the opening of its Porto-Franco free customs zone, established under Presidential Resolution No. PP-50 of February 9, 2026.

    According to recent reports, described as Central Asia's first free customs zone of its kind, Porto-Franco supports duty-free storage and processing of international goods alongside upgraded ground handling equipment. Together, commercial autonomy and customs-free handling give Navoi a distinct institutional foundation as a dedicated freight hub.

    Uzbekistan's air cargo market has expanded rapidly, creating a strong commercial backdrop for Navoi's push. Air cargo volume in Uzbekistan climbed 182% between 2019 and 2024 before rising another 33% in the first half of 2026, per Trend News Agency. That sustained growth reflects rising trade flows across Central Asia and growing demand for reliable transit links between Asia and Europe.

    According to recent reports, geopolitical disruptions in the Middle East have added urgency to that shift by straining traditional southern routing options. As conflict-related closures and airspace restrictions affect Gulf hubs and Middle Eastern corridors, freight forwarders and airlines have increasingly looked toward Central Asian transit routes as an alternative connection point between Asian manufacturing centers and European markets.

    According to recent reports, uzbekistan sits directly along that overland and aerial corridor, making it an ideal location under these circumstances. Within Uzbekistan, Navoi is being positioned as a dedicated cargo and multimodal logistics hub and is not necessarily competing head-to-head with Tashkent's passenger-heavy gateway.

    Connecting air freighters with regional rail and road networks allows shipments to move smoothly across Eurasia and keeps heavy freighter traffic away from crowded capital-city passenger operations. For cargo operators, that separation makes Navoi a cleaner fit for high-volume transit.

    It has been revealed that backing up Navoi's hub ambitions can only be achieved with improved capacity on the ground as freighter traffic scales up, as detailed in reporting from Air Cargo Week. That capacity is well on its way, with a latest 172,223-square-foot (16,000-square-meter) cargo terminal under construction at the airport, paired with fuel storage expanded to 16,535 short tons (15,000 metric tons) to support long-range widebody turnarounds.

    Those upgrades give cargo operators dedicated warehouse space and reliable uplift in a way that does not strain existing apron operations. Technical and maintenance support is also part of the buildout roadmap as Navoi prepares for heavier widebody use. According to Trend News Agency, plans include a dedicated aircraft maintenance and painting center for widebody aircraft targeted for completion by 2028.

    Recent findings suggest that this will expand local technical capabilities alongside cargo handling. Ultimately, having heavy maintenance and paint capacity closer to the corridor reduces repositioning overhead for operators. Those investments tie directly to ambitious operational targets set for the end of the decade, highlighted in coverage by UzDaily and Trend News Agency.

    Recent findings suggest that navoi is aiming for 7,000 annual flights and 49,604 short tons (45,000 metric tons) of cargo by 2030 as commercial agreements and logistics partnerships scale up. Hitting those milestones, though, will all depend on the planned terminals, fuel capacity, and 2028 maintenance facilities and whether these can provide steady daily throughput.

    Cargolux brings a specialized all-cargo fleet built around the 747 family, with a 30-aircraft lineup of Boeing 747-400F and 747-8F freighters detailed in Trans.ru's report on the permit and Cargolux's fleet overview. What makes the 747 particularly unique and well-suited to cargo operations is its nose-loading capability.

    Nose-loading widebody freighters are well suited to bulky, outsized, and high-value shipments moving along Eurasian corridors where straight-in main-deck loading saves handling time and supports long-range trunk lift. Even with the November 17, 2026 approval in hand, key operational details remain unannounced within UzDaily's coverage of the permit and Kapital.uz's report.

    Sources indicate that neither a launch date nor flight frequency has been disclosed, and public reporting has not yet confirmed exact routings, payload allocations, or how Navoi flights will link into Cargolux's broader European network out of Luxembourg. From the viewpoint of cargo planners and shippers, that gap means the permit marks a regulatory green light rather than an immediate timetable.

    Until schedules and routing structures are published, market watchers will look to subsequent announcements, whether that be from media outlets or the airline itself, to see whether Navoi will be a dedicated regional stop, a multi-sector transit point, or an overflow hub for high-density freight.

    Navoi's pure-play cargo and multimodal positioning sets it apart from Tashkent as well as other Central Asian and nearby Caucasus logistics hubs competing for Asia–Europe freight, as examined by Air Cargo Week and Seetao. Other airports in the region generally rely on belly hold capacity tied to passenger schedules.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, Navoi focuses on dedicated freighter turnarounds backed by road and rail links across Central Asia and China–Europe trade lanes. Across the wider region, airports and logistics corridors in Central Asia and the Caucasus are expanding capacity simultaneously to capture shifting transit flows, as covered in Air Cargo Week's regional cargo capacity analysis.

    According to recent reports, competition centers on customs efficiency, ground handling speed, and seamless links between air corridors and overland rail or trucking routes. Airports such as Baku Heydar Aliyev Airport (GYD) already have established cargo demand, supported by Baku-based Silk Way West as well as the presence of operators such as Cargolux. Overall, Navoi is looking to be in a really good position to establish itself strongly in the global cargo network.

    It has been revealed that as such, it may not be long before more operators, in addition to Cargolux, look to cement their operations in this Central Asian hub. Regional hub rivalry comes down to execution and reliability, and Navoi's infrastructure growth epitomizes this. Hubs that pair multimodal connectivity with predictable clearance and turnaround times stand the best chance of holding onto Asia–Europe cargo once routing choices stabilize.

    Cargolux's November 17, 2026 permit to operate Boeing 747F flights to Navoi International Airport is a major milestone for Central Asian aviation, a decision that highlights how shifting trade corridors, Middle East airspace disruptions, and hub design are reshaping Asia–Europe air cargo.

    Industry observers note that with commercial autonomy and the Porto-Franco free customs zone, alongside a 30-aircraft 747-400F and 747-8F operator, Navoi has an incredible opening to compete as a dedicated freighter hub rather than an afterthought behind Tashkent. Going from regulatory approval to sustained commercial volume will depend on decision-making across both airlines and airport planners over the coming years.

    While launch dates, frequencies, routings, payloads, and European network ties remain unannounced, Navoi's 172,223-square-foot (16,000-square-meter) cargo terminal buildout, 16,535-short-ton (15,000-metric-ton) fuel storage expansion, 2028 widebody maintenance and painting center, and 2030 goals of 7,000 annual flights and 49,604 short tons (45,000 metric tons) of cargo set clear benchmarks.

    Recent findings suggest that ultimately, whether Navoi becomes a permanent fixture on Cargolux's 747 map will come down to real-world performance when up against rival hubs across Central Asia and the Caucasus. If multimodal rail and road links, customs clearance, and widebody ground support deliver consistent turnarounds as traffic grows, an airport most flyers have never heard of could support a major link in Eurasian cargo logistics.

    It's that time of year again: Holiday gift-giving is on the mind, travelers are planning 2027 (and last-minute 2026) trips, and Black Friday hotel deals are in full swing. Those looking to score the best bang for their buck on hotel deals this year will find that there are already tons of excellent offers from some of your favorite brands, whether you're looking for a beachy Caribbean escape or a ski vacation in Aspen. Are you the type of person who stays loyal to their favorite brands, like World of Hyatt and Marriott Bonvoy? Or more the traveler who enjoys scrolling through endless options on travel booking sites like Expedia and Booking.com? Whatever your method, there are tons of ways to save.

    This Black Friday, many hotels are offering generous discounts, reward point bonuses, complimentary amenities, and flexible travel windows that will allow you to plan well into 2027. These limited-time holiday savings will let you elevate your upcoming getaways while staying within your budget, making this one of the smartest times to plan next year’s vacation. If you’ve been waiting for the right moment to secure your next stay, there's no better time than right now. But don't wait! While many brands have sales running through next week, you'll want to book as early as possible to ensure your first-choice properties and dates are available.

    Sources indicate that booking.com's Black Friday sale is back for another year, which means you can score up to 40% off hotel stays from now through December 2. Whether you're headed on a once-in-a-lifetime bucket-list trip to Japan (hotel deals in Tokyo start at just $31 per night), or are taking a quick weekend break in Vegas (hotel deals in Vegas start at just $57 per night), you can save major while traveling more. Travelers can also get up to 25% off car rentals, 20% off experiences, 15% off airport transfers, and up to $2,000 in onboard cruise credits.

Expedia makes it easy to proposal every aspect of your trip right on its platform, from where you'll stay to the excursions you'll enjoy once you get there. Book by December 3 to enjoy deals in top destinations like Nashville, Miami, and Rome, and keep an eye out for Flash Deals: On Black Friday (November 27), Cyber Monday (November 30), and Travel Tuesday (December 1), select stays will be up to 75% off. Pro tip: It's worth becoming a One Key loyalty member if you haven't already (it's free!) to ensure that you always get the absolute best prices on offer.
